body.title: Contrast & weighting: the exam synthesis
body.html:
Image contrast in conventional spin echo is set by two knobs: TR governs how much T1 weighting you get, and TE governs how much T2 weighting. Combine them:

  • Short TR / short TE → T1-weighted. Fat and white matter bright; fluid (CSF) dark.
  • Long TR / long TE → T2-weighted. Fluid bright. This is where most pathology (extra water) shows.
  • Long TR / short TE → proton density. Both weightings minimised; signal tracks tissue water content.

Inversion recovery adds a preparatory 180° pulse and a TI. Choosing TI at a tissue's null point suppresses it: STIR (short TI ≈ 0.69·T1 of fat) nulls fat; FLAIR (long TI ≈ 2000-2500 ms) nulls CSF so periventricular lesions aren't hidden. Gradient echo uses a flip angle instead of a 180° refocuser and is sensitive to T2* (susceptibility). Gadolinium shortens T1, so enhancing tissue is bright on T1, which marks blood-brain-barrier breakdown.

The fastest read: find the fluid (ventricles, eyeballs). Dark fluid → T1. Bright fluid → T2. Bright everything-but-fluid → FLAIR.
keypoints: TR controls T1 weighting; TE controls T2 weighting.
Short TR/short TE = T1; long TR/long TE = T2; long TR/short TE = PD.
STIR nulls fat (TI ≈ 0.69·T1 fat); FLAIR nulls CSF (long TI).
Gradient echo → flip angle, T2* sensitive.
Gadolinium shortens T1 → bright on T1 at BBB breakdown.
body.worked_example: You pull up a lumbar spine protocol and see a sagittal sequence with TR 500 ms and TE 20 ms alongside a second sagittal sequence with TR 3500 ms and TE 110 ms. The first is T1-weighted: the short TR gives longitudinal magnetization little time to recover between excitations, so tissue with a short T1, like fat and marrow, regrows the most magnetization and looks bright, while CSF, with its long T1, stays dark. The second is T2-weighted: the long TR lets essentially every tissue fully recover before the next pulse, which erases T1 differences, and the long TE then lets transverse magnetization decay, so tissue with a long T2, like CSF and edema, still has signal left and looks bright. A disc herniation with surrounding edema can be easy to miss on the T1 image, where fat dominates the contrast, but it stands out against the dark disc and cord on the T2 image. If a third sequence paired a long TR with a short TE, both T1 and T2 weighting would be minimized and the image would instead track proton density, the raw concentration of mobile hydrogen in each tissue.
memory_hooks: Short TR and short TE favor fat, long TR and long TE favor fluid. Find the CSF: dark is T1, bright is T2.
TR controls how much T1 shows through and TE controls how much T2 shows through. Cancel both (long TR, short TE) and what's left is proton density.
A nulling TI is about 0.69 times the T1 of the tissue being suppressed, which is why STIR (short TI, nulls fat) and FLAIR (long TI, nulls CSF) use such different TI values.
exam_traps: STIR nulls anything with fat's short T1, not just fat. Gadolinium shortens T1 into that same range, so STIR will null enhancement too, which is why STIR is not paired with contrast.
Long TR alone does not make a sequence T2-weighted. Long TR with a short TE removes T1 weighting but adds proton density weighting instead, not T2.
A gradient echo image looks T2-like but its dark-blood and susceptibility artifact come from T2 star, which includes local field inhomogeneity on top of true T2 decay, not T2 alone.

body.title: Image quality: SNR, CNR, resolution & the trade-offs
body.html:
SNR (signal-to-noise) rises with voxel volume (bigger voxels = more signal), with √NEX (averages), with lower receiver bandwidth, with field strength, and with better coils. CNR (contrast-to-noise) is the difference in signal between two tissues over the noise, and it is what actually makes a lesion visible.

Spatial resolution is set by voxel size: a finer matrix or smaller FOV or thinner slice = smaller voxels = more detail, but each holds less signal, so SNR falls. That is the fundamental resolution ↔ SNR trade at fixed scan time.

Scan time (2D SE) = TR × phase-encode steps × NEX. So doubling the phase matrix doubles both resolution-in-that-axis and scan time. Everything is a four-way balance of SNR, resolution, coverage, and time.

Two efficiency levers: the Ernst angle maximises GRE signal for a given TR/T1, and parallel imaging (SENSE/GRAPPA) buys speed at an SNR cost of g·√R (the g-factor, worst centrally).
keypoints: SNR ∝ voxel volume × √NEX; lower bandwidth and higher field raise it.
Finer matrix / smaller FOV / thinner slice = more resolution, less SNR.
Scan time (2D SE) = TR × phase steps × NEX.
CNR (not raw SNR) determines lesion conspicuity.
Parallel imaging costs SNR by g·√R (g-factor).
body.worked_example: You are imaging a small joint with a 3 mm slice, a 256 phase-encode matrix, 1 NEX, and the images are noisy. Thinning the slice to 2 mm to reduce partial-volume blur cuts voxel volume by a third, and since SNR is proportional to voxel volume, SNR falls by roughly that same fraction. To claw some signal back you average twice, going to 2 NEX. Because SNR improves only with the square root of the number of averages, that recovers about the square root of 2, not a full doubling, and it doubles scan time, since 2D spin echo scan time equals TR times phase-encode steps times NEX. If instead you had doubled the phase matrix to 512 steps to gain in-plane resolution, you would halve the phase-encode pixel dimension, taking another SNR hit from the smaller voxel, while also doubling scan time directly, because phase steps multiply straight into the scan-time formula. Resolution, SNR, and time are locked together: buying back one always costs one of the other two.
memory_hooks: SNR scales directly with voxel volume but only with the square root of NEX. Halve the voxel and you lose a full factor of SNR; you need four times the averages to win it back.
For 2D spin echo, scan time equals TR times phase-encode steps times NEX. Only the phase direction adds time; more frequency-encode samples sharpen resolution for free.
CNR, not raw SNR, is what makes a lesion visible. A high-SNR image with poor tissue contrast can still hide pathology that a noisier, higher-contrast image shows clearly.
exam_traps: Increasing the frequency-encode matrix does not add scan time, but increasing the phase-encode matrix does, directly and linearly. Don't confuse the two directions.

Parallel imaging (SENSE or GRAPPA) buys speed by skipping phase-encode lines, but the SNR cost is the g-factor times the square root of the acceleration R, and the g-factor penalty is worst at the center of the FOV, not spread evenly.
Raising receiver bandwidth shortens scan time and reduces chemical-shift artifact, but it lowers SNR because a wider bandwidth admits more noise per sample. It is not a free efficiency gain.

body.title: MR safety: the exam-focused overview
body.html:
MRI has no ionising radiation, but three fields are always present. The static field is always on: its danger is the projectile (missile) effect on ferromagnetic objects, plus benign transient bioeffects (dizziness, a metallic taste, magnetophosphenes) at high field. The gradients switch fast: their dB/dt can cause peripheral nerve stimulation, and their acoustic noise (up to ~120 dB) mandates hearing protection. The RF deposits energy as heat (SAR, W/kg), risking burns from looped cables or skin-to-skin contact.

Facilities use four zones (I public → IV magnet room, most restricted). Everyone is screened; implants are checked against MR-safe / MR-conditional / MR-unsafe labelling (an MR-conditional device is safe only under the stated field/SAR/slew limits). A quench boils off helium, which is vented outside, but a failed vent risks oxygen displacement (asphyxiation) and frostbite. Gadolinium in severe renal impairment carries a risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.
keypoints: Three fields: static (projectile), gradient (PNS + acoustic), RF (SAR/burns).
Zone IV = magnet room, most restricted; no ferromagnetic items.
MR-conditional = safe ONLY under the stated conditions.
Quench → helium boil-off → possible oxygen displacement.
Gadolinium + severe renal impairment → NSF risk.
body.worked_example: A patient in a wheelchair with a small pocketknife left in a jacket pocket is brought toward the scanner room by a family member who was never screened. The knife is drawn toward the bore and becomes a projectile, the classic ferromagnetic missile effect from the always-on static field. The correct workflow is that everyone entering Zone III or IV, staff, patients, and visitors alike, is screened with a metal detector and a verbal/written questionnaire before crossing into Zone IV, and only MR-trained, screened staff supervise anyone in Zone IV. The static field is never off, even during a power outage, so screening has to happen at the zone boundary every single time, not just once at intake.
memory_hooks: Four zones, increasing restriction: Zone I public access, Zone II screening/reception, Zone III controlled (screened persons only), Zone IV the magnet room itself.

Three fields, three hazards: static field causes the projectile effect (always on), gradients cause peripheral nerve stimulation and loud acoustic noise (dB/dt, switching fast), RF deposits heat measured as SAR and can burn from loops or skin contact.

MR Safe, MR Conditional, MR Unsafe are the only three labels; MR Conditional is safe only under the specific field strength, SAR, and gradient slew-rate conditions on its label, so you verify the label and the scanner parameters every time, never assume from a similar device.
exam_traps: A quench vents helium outside the building by design; the danger is a failed or blocked vent path leading to oxygen displacement (asphyxiation risk) and cold burns in the magnet room, so a quench is a planned safety response, not a routine event and not itself the hazard.

SAR-related burns most often come from looped cables or skin-to-skin contact points completing a conductive loop, not from the implant itself; padding cables away from skin and preventing loops is basic technologist practice on every patient.

Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis is a gadolinium contrast risk tied to severe renal impairment, not a static-field or RF hazard; it belongs with screening for renal function, not with zone or projectile safety.

body.title: Patient care: screening to monitoring
body.html:
Screen before every scan (status changes): implants, pacemakers, aneurysm clips, cochlear implants, neurostimulators, and metal. A history of metalwork/grinding needs orbital radiographs to exclude an intra-orbital fragment. Prepare the patient: remove all ferromagnetic items, gown as needed, explain the loud noise, and give hearing protection.

Position for signal and comfort: centre the anatomy in the coil at isocentre, immobilise to reduce motion, and hand over the call/squeeze device. For contrast, check eGFR and prior reactions, obtain consent, and know the plan for an acute reaction (hives/wheeze/hypotension → stop, help, ABCs, epinephrine for anaphylaxis). Avoid gadolinium in pregnancy unless essential.

Monitor throughout: keep verbal contact, manage claustrophobia (reassurance, call system, wide/open bore, sedation), and use only MR-safe monitoring equipment for sedated or unstable patients.
keypoints: Screen before every scan; orbital radiographs for metal-in-eye history.
Hearing protection for every patient.
Contrast: check eGFR, consent, know reaction management (epinephrine for anaphylaxis).
Avoid gadolinium in pregnancy unless essential.
Monitor continuously; MR-safe equipment only.
body.worked_example: A patient scheduled for a contrast-enhanced lumbar spine MRI reports a history of working with a metal grinder years ago and has never had an orbital X-ray to clear metal fragments. Screening also turns up reduced kidney function on a recent lab result. The correct sequence is to hold the contrast-enhanced order and first obtain orbital radiographs to rule out a retained intra-orbital metallic fragment, since an occult fragment near the globe can move or heat during scanning; separately, the technologist checks the patient's eGFR against facility policy for gadolinium and discusses the finding with the ordering provider, because severe renal impairment raises the risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis. Screening is not a one-time chart review, it is repeated before this specific scan because implant and health status can change between visits.
memory_hooks: Screen every single time, not just once: implants, devices, pregnancy status, renal function, and metal exposure history can all change visit to visit.
Metalworking or grinding history plus no prior orbital imaging means get orbital radiographs before scanning, to rule out an intra-orbital metallic fragment.

For a contrast reaction, start with the basics: stop the injection, get help, support airway-breathing-circulation, and give epinephrine for anaphylaxis; know this sequence cold, it is the first-line response.
exam_traps: Claustrophobia management (reassurance, call/squeeze device, open or wide-bore magnet, sedation when needed) is a comfort and completion issue, not a contraindication to scanning by itself.

Gadolinium is avoided in pregnancy unless the information is essential to care and cannot wait, because it crosses the placenta; this is a risk-benefit decision with the ordering provider, not an absolute rule against ever scanning a pregnant patient.

Only MR-safe or MR-conditional monitoring equipment, matched to the specific scanner conditions, may enter the magnet room for a sedated or unstable patient; standard ward monitors and infusion pumps are not substitutes.

body.prompt: A spin-echo sequence uses a short TR and a short TE. What weighting results?
options: T1-weighted
T2-weighted
Proton density
Diffusion-weighted
body.explain: Short TR emphasises T1 recovery differences; short TE minimises T2 decay. The result is T1 weighting: fat and white matter bright, fluid dark.

body.prompt: STIR suppresses fat by choosing an inversion time (TI) equal to approximately:
options: 0.69 times the T1 of fat, its null point
The full T1 of water at that field strength
Roughly twice the echo time TE
About half the repetition time TR
body.explain: In inversion recovery, a tissue is nulled when TI ≈ 0.69·T1 of that tissue. STIR sets a short TI at fat's null point, so fat gives no signal, useful where spectral fat-sat fails (off-isocentre, metal, poor shim).

body.prompt: On a FLAIR image, why does CSF appear dark despite the heavy T2 weighting?
options: A long inversion time nulls the CSF signal
A very short echo time keeps CSF dark
Injected gadolinium suppresses the CSF signal
CSF has an unusually short T2 value
body.explain: FLAIR is an inversion-recovery sequence with a long TI (~2000-2500 ms) set to CSF's null point, so fluid is dark while the underlying image stays T2-weighted, so periventricular lesions no longer hide in bright CSF.

body.prompt: Gadolinium makes enhancing tissue bright on T1-weighted images because it:
options: Shortens the T1 of nearby tissue where it collects
Gives off its own strong MR signal directly
Is intrinsically bright like fluid on T2
Suppresses the surrounding fat signal
body.explain: Gadolinium is paramagnetic and shortens local T1, so tissue it reaches brightens on T1 weighting. It only crosses a broken blood-brain barrier, so enhancement marks BBB breakdown (tumour, active inflammation).

body.prompt: Increasing NEX (signal averages) from 1 to 4 changes SNR by roughly what factor, and at what time cost?
options: Doubles SNR at four times the scan time
Quadruples SNR at twice the scan time
Doubles SNR at twice the scan time
No change in SNR at any time cost
body.explain: SNR scales with the square root of the number of averages, so 4 averages give √4 = 2× SNR, but scan time scales linearly, so it costs 4× the time. Averaging is an expensive way to buy SNR.

body.prompt: Lowering the receiver bandwidth raises SNR but worsens which artifact (and lengthens the minimum TE)?
options: Chemical shift
Motion ghosting
Zipper
Aliasing
body.explain: A narrower bandwidth spends longer sampling each echo (more signal, higher SNR) but spreads fat and water further apart in the readout direction (worse chemical-shift misregistration) and forces a longer minimum TE.

body.prompt: For a 2-D spin-echo acquisition, total scan time equals:
options: TR times phase-encode steps times NEX
TE times the full matrix times NEX
TR times TE times the slice count
TR times the frequency-encode steps
body.explain: Each TR collects one phase-encode line; you need one per phase step, repeated for each average. So time = TR × (phase steps) × NEX. Frequency encoding is free (within the readout), which is why the phase matrix (not the frequency matrix) drives scan time.

body.prompt: The centre of k-space predominantly encodes:
options: Overall image contrast and signal
Fine edge detail and resolution
The receiver bandwidth
The slice position
body.explain: Low spatial frequencies (k-space centre) carry the bulk of the signal and overall contrast; the periphery carries high spatial frequencies: edges and fine detail (resolution). This is why partial-Fourier and centric ordering behave as they do.

body.prompt: Aliasing (wraparound) in the phase-encode direction occurs when:
options: The FOV is smaller than the object being imaged
The echo time is far too long for the tissue
The magnet is shimmed poorly over the FOV
The flip angle rises above the Ernst angle
body.explain: Anatomy outside the phase-encode FOV is under-sampled (below Nyquist) and folds back to the opposite side. Fixes: enlarge the FOV, apply no-phase-wrap (phase oversampling), or saturate the out-of-FOV tissue.

body.prompt: An implant labelled 'MR Conditional' means it is:
options: Safe to scan only within the stated conditions
Considered safe in any MRI scanner at all
Never to be brought in for scanning
Made only of non-metallic materials
body.explain: MR-Conditional means safe only within stated limits, for example up to a given field strength, SAR, and gradient slew rate, sometimes with a required scan mode. MR-Safe = no known hazards in any MR environment; MR-Unsafe = keep out of Zone IV.

body.prompt: Moving into a 3-T bore, a patient reports a brief metallic taste and mild dizziness. This is best explained as:
options: A benign, transient bioeffect of the static field
An allergic reaction to gadolinium
Peripheral nerve stimulation from the gradients
The onset of an RF burn
body.explain: Movement through a strong static field can transiently stimulate the vestibular system and tongue (a metallic taste), causing brief dizziness, benign and self-limited. It is unrelated to gradients (PNS), RF (heating), or contrast.

body.prompt: Which practice best prevents RF (SAR) burns during a scan?
options: Keep cables straight and padded, uncross limbs
Raise the receiver bandwidth for the scan
Lower the static magnetic field strength
Shorten the repetition time TR
body.explain: RF burns arise where induced currents concentrate: conductive loops (looped cables) or skin-to-skin contact forming a loop. Straighten and pad cables, insulate the patient from the bore, and uncross limbs. Bandwidth/field/TR don't address the loop.

body.prompt: A pregnant MRI technologist may:
options: Keep working in the MRI suite but leave the bore in scans
Not enter Zone III or IV under any circumstance
Work only on scanners at 1.5 T or below
Work only while wearing a lead apron for shielding
body.explain: Guidelines permit pregnant staff to work in and around the MRI suite; the usual precaution is not to remain inside the bore during active scanning. MRI uses no ionising radiation, so lead aprons are irrelevant.

body.prompt: The first-line drug for a gadolinium-induced anaphylactic reaction is:
options: Epinephrine (adrenaline)
Diphenhydramine alone
Furosemide
Metformin
body.explain: Anaphylaxis is treated first with epinephrine, alongside airway/breathing/circulation support and calling for help. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts, not the first-line agent for true anaphylaxis.

body.prompt: Which measure most helps a claustrophobic patient tolerate the exam?
options: Reassurance with feet-first entry or a wide bore
Raising the SAR to finish the scan faster
Removing the call button to reduce distraction
Turning off the patient's hearing protection
body.explain: Reassurance and steady communication, the call/squeeze system, feet-first or prone entry, mirrors/prism glasses, a wide/open-bore magnet, or sedation all help. Never remove the patient's means to signal distress.

body.prompt: Before administering gadolinium, the single most important lab value to review is:
options: eGFR as a measure of renal function
The fasting blood glucose level
The serum potassium level
The haemoglobin A1c value
body.explain: Renal function (eGFR) drives the risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis with gadolinium. Severe impairment prompts avoiding contrast or using the lowest dose of a macrocyclic agent. Also confirm prior reactions and consent.

body.title: Pulse sequences: SE, FSE, GRE, EPI and how they are built
body.html:
A pulse sequence is a timed recipe of RF pulses and gradients that fills k-space line by line. The families you must recognise:

  • Spin echo (SE): a 90° excitation then a 180° refocusing pulse. The 180° cancels static field inhomogeneity, so SE is T2 (not T2*) weighted and robust to susceptibility, though one echo per TR makes it slow.
  • Fast/turbo spin echo (FSE/TSE): multiple 180° pulses after each excitation collect an echo train (ETL). Scan time drops by roughly the ETL factor. The effective TE is set by when the centre of k-space is filled, not by the first echo. Long trains blur and make fat stay bright.
  • Gradient echo (GRE): a single flip angle with no 180°; the echo is formed by a gradient reversal, so residual field inhomogeneity is not refocused and GRE is T2* weighted. Spoiled GRE gives T1/T2* contrast, while balanced SSFP keeps transverse magnetisation for a bright-fluid T2/T1 ratio image.
  • Echo-planar imaging (EPI): fills all (or many) k-space lines after a single excitation, the basis of DWI and fMRI. It is extremely fast but very sensitive to susceptibility, causing geometric distortion and signal dropout near air and bone.

Diffusion (DWI) adds paired motion-probing gradients scaled by the b-value; tissue where water cannot move (acute stroke) stays bright while the ADC map is dark. The single organising idea is that how you refocus the echo (180° versus gradient) and how many lines you read per excitation together set the contrast, the speed, and the artifacts.
keypoints: SE uses a 180 refocuser for true T2: susceptibility-robust but slow.
FSE reads an echo train (ETL), cutting time by the ETL factor; effective TE is when the k-space centre is filled.
GRE has no 180, so it is T2* weighted; spoiled gives T1/T2*, balanced SSFP gives bright fluid.
EPI fills k-space in one shot: fast (DWI and fMRI) but prone to geometric distortion.
DWI: restricted diffusion is bright on DWI and dark on the ADC map.
body.worked_example: A patient has a hip replacement and you must choose between a fast spin echo and a gradient echo proton density sequence to evaluate the bone next to the hardware. Gradient echo has no 180 degree refocusing pulse, so the local field distortion the metal creates around it is never cancelled, and the image shows a large signal void with visible geometric warping near the implant. Fast spin echo runs a whole train of 180 degree pulses, and each one refocuses the dephasing that metal induced since the last pulse, so the artifact shrinks dramatically. The right choice for periprosthetic imaging is fast spin echo, or a dedicated metal artifact reduction sequence built on it, because the refocusing pulse train is what tames the T2 star dephasing that a gradient echo sequence cannot correct.
memory_hooks: Spin echo and fast spin echo both refocus with a 180, so both read out true T2. Gradient echo skips the 180, so it reads out T2 star instead.
EPI is the one shot sequence: one excitation fills most or all of k-space, which is why it is fast for diffusion and functional imaging but also the most distortion prone sequence.
Effective TE in fast spin echo is set by whichever echo fills the center of k-space, not by the first echo in the train.
exam_traps: Do not confuse T2 with T2 star. T2 star is always shorter than T2 because it includes magnet inhomogeneity dephasing that the 180 degree pulse in spin echo and fast spin echo cancels out; gradient echo has no way to cancel it.

A longer echo train shortens fast spin echo scan time, but it also blurs detail and lets fat stay bright even at a long effective TE, which is different from conventional spin echo where fat is dark at long TE.

Diffusion weighted imaging and the ADC map read oppositely: restricted diffusion, such as acute stroke, is bright on the DWI image but dark on the ADC map. Mixing those two up reverses the clinical read.

body.prompt: Compared with conventional spin echo, fast/turbo spin echo (FSE/TSE) shortens scan time mainly by:
options: Collecting several k-space lines per TR in an echo train
Using a considerably larger flip angle each TR
Omitting the 180-degree refocusing pulses entirely
Lowering the receiver bandwidth substantially
body.explain: FSE applies multiple 180-degree refocusing pulses after each excitation, collecting an echo train. Scan time falls by roughly the echo-train length, because that many phase-encode lines are filled per TR.

body.prompt: In an FSE acquisition, the effective TE that determines image contrast is set by:
options: The echo whose data fills the centre of k-space
The first echo that is played out in the echo train
The final echo played out at the end of the train
The simple average of all the echo times used
body.explain: Contrast is dominated by the low spatial frequencies at the centre of k-space. Whichever echo is played out while the centre is being filled sets the effective TE, regardless of the other echoes in the train.

body.prompt: Gradient-echo sequences are more sensitive to susceptibility (T2*) than spin echo because they:
options: Lack a 180-degree pulse to refocus inhomogeneity
Use a much longer repetition time overall
Always acquire a much smaller image matrix
Deposit far more RF energy into the tissue
body.explain: A gradient reversal reforms the echo but does not cancel static field inhomogeneity the way a 180-degree pulse does. So GRE decays with T2* and blooms on blood, calcium and metal, which SWI exploits but which becomes a liability near air.

body.prompt: Single-shot echo-planar imaging (EPI), the workhorse of DWI and fMRI, is most limited by:
options: Geometric distortion and dropout from susceptibility
An excessively long total acquisition time
An inability to generate any T2 contrast at all
A required 180-degree pulse for every line
body.explain: EPI reads all of k-space after one excitation, so it is very fast but accumulates phase errors from off-resonance, producing geometric distortion and signal dropout near air and bone interfaces (skull base, sinuses, posterior fossa).

body.title: Reading pathology: where lesions hide and what lights them up
body.html:
Most pathology adds water (oedema, inflammation, many tumours), so it is bright on T2 and on FLAIR. Because FLAIR nulls CSF, periventricular and cortical lesions no longer hide in bright fluid. A short checklist of the sequences that reveal specific disease:

  • DWI and ADC: restricted diffusion is bright on DWI and dark on ADC. This is the signature of acute infarct, and also of abscess and hypercellular tumour. Beware T2 shine-through: always check the ADC to confirm true restriction.
  • Post-gadolinium T1: enhancement marks blood-brain-barrier breakdown such as tumour, active demyelination, or infection. Patterns matter (a ring-enhancing lesion suggests abscess, glioblastoma or metastasis).
  • GRE and SWI: blooming (exaggerated dark signal) reveals blood products, calcium and iron through susceptibility.

Finally, know what is bright on T1 without contrast: fat, subacute haemorrhage (methaemoglobin), melanin (melanoma metastases), proteinaceous or highly concentrated fluid, and slow flow. Recognising these keeps you from mistaking intrinsic T1 brightness for enhancement.
keypoints: Most pathology is extra water, so it is bright on T2 and FLAIR (FLAIR nulls CSF).
Restricted diffusion is bright on DWI and dark on ADC: acute stroke, abscess, dense tumour.
Post-gadolinium enhancement marks blood-brain-barrier breakdown.
GRE and SWI blooming reveals blood, calcium and iron.
Intrinsically T1-bright: fat, subacute blood, melanin, proteinaceous fluid.
body.worked_example: A 68-year-old presents with sudden left-sided weakness three hours from symptom onset. The right MCA territory shows a focal area that is bright on DWI and dark on ADC, confirming true restricted diffusion rather than T2 shine-through, which is the signature of acute infarct. The FLAIR sequence in the same region is still nearly normal, because vasogenic edema and FLAIR hyperintensity typically lag several hours behind the diffusion abnormality, so a DWI-FLAIR mismatch supports that the stroke is still within an early treatment window. A GRE or SWI sequence is added to exclude hemorrhage before any decision about thrombolysis, since blooming susceptibility artifact there would mean a bleed rather than a candidate for lytic therapy. No enhancement is expected yet on post-gadolinium T1, because blood-brain-barrier breakdown from infarct typically takes a few days to appear.
memory_hooks: Bright on DWI and dark on ADC is true restriction. Bright on DWI with a normal or bright ADC is T2 shine-through, not a true acute infarct.
DWI lights up within minutes of stroke onset, but FLAIR takes hours to catch up, so a DWI-FLAIR mismatch is a clue to how fresh the stroke is.
Blooming on GRE or SWI means blood, calcium, or iron, and the dark spot on the image is always bigger than the true lesion.
exam_traps: T2 shine-through: a chronic lesion can look bright on DWI simply because it is bright on T2, not because diffusion is restricted. Always confirm with the ADC map, which should be dark for a true acute infarct.

A ring-enhancing lesion is not specific to one diagnosis. Abscess, glioblastoma, and metastasis can all show this pattern, so additional clues such as restricted diffusion in the abscess cavity are needed to tell them apart.

T1 brightness without contrast, from fat, subacute blood, melanin, or concentrated proteinaceous fluid, can be mistaken for enhancement. Always compare to the pre-contrast T1 or use fat saturation to confirm true enhancement.

body.prompt: An acute cerebral infarct classically appears:
options: Bright on DWI and dark on the ADC map
Dark on DWI and bright on the ADC map
Bright on both DWI and the ADC map
Visible only after gadolinium is given
body.explain: Cytotoxic oedema restricts water diffusion within minutes of infarction: bright on DWI, dark on ADC. This appears well before T2 and FLAIR changes, which is why DWI is the key stroke sequence.

body.prompt: Which lesion is intrinsically BRIGHT on a T1-weighted image WITHOUT any gadolinium?
options: Subacute haematoma with methaemoglobin
A simple cyst filled with clear CSF
An area of acute cytotoxic oedema
A purely calcified nodule with no blood
body.explain: Methaemoglobin in subacute blood shortens T1, so it is bright on unenhanced T1, as are fat, melanin and proteinaceous fluid. Simple fluid is dark on T1, and calcium is usually dark on standard sequences.

body.prompt: Why is FLAIR preferred over standard T2 for detecting periventricular MS plaques?
options: It nulls bright CSF so periventricular lesions show
It is fundamentally a T1-weighted sequence type
It selectively suppresses the fat signal only
It is much faster to acquire than plain T2
body.explain: FLAIR is an inversion-recovery sequence with a long TI that nulls CSF while keeping T2 weighting. Periventricular plaques that would blend into bright ventricular fluid on T2 become conspicuous.

body.prompt: A focus that blooms (looks larger and darker) on gradient-echo or SWI most likely represents:
options: Blood products, calcium or iron deposition
Simple watery fluid in a cavity
Ordinary subcutaneous or marrow fat
Fast-flowing arterial blood in a vessel
body.explain: Susceptibility from haemosiderin, calcium or iron dephases spins and exaggerates the dark signal on T2*-weighted GRE and SWI, called blooming. It is how microhaemorrhages and mineralisation are detected.

body.title: Flow, function and artifacts: MRA methods and the artifacts to name
body.html:
Imaging flow. Three ways to see vessels without catheters:

  • Time-of-flight (TOF) MRA: stationary tissue is saturated by rapid RF, while fresh inflowing blood is unsaturated and bright (flow-related enhancement). It fails for in-plane flow because those spins saturate, so use thin slabs perpendicular to the vessel. A saturation band on one side selects arteries versus veins.
  • Phase-contrast (PC) MRA: bipolar gradients give moving spins a net phase proportional to velocity. You set a VENC (encoding velocity); if the true velocity exceeds VENC, the phase wraps and you get velocity aliasing. PC also quantifies flow and direction.
  • Contrast-enhanced MRA: gadolinium shortens blood T1 for a fast, flow-independent angiogram, where timing the bolus to the arterial phase is everything.

Artifacts to recognise by name: motion produces ghosting along the phase-encode direction (pulsatile flow ghosts too, so a saturation band or gating helps); chemical shift lies along the frequency direction (worse at high field or low bandwidth); aliasing or wraparound occurs when the FOV is smaller than the object in the phase direction; Gibbs or truncation appears as parallel ringing lines at high-contrast borders (reduce with a finer matrix); susceptibility distorts near metal or air, worst on GRE and EPI; and the zipper comes from stray RF.
keypoints: TOF MRA: inflowing unsaturated spins are bright; it fails for in-plane flow.
Phase contrast: velocity above VENC gives aliasing; PC also quantifies flow direction.
Motion and pulsatile-flow ghosts propagate along the PHASE-encode direction.
Chemical shift is in the FREQUENCY direction; worse at high field or low bandwidth.
Gibbs or truncation is ringing at sharp borders; reduce it with a higher matrix.
body.worked_example: An axial T2-weighted image of the abdomen shows a bright band of ghosting running across the whole image in the anterior to posterior direction, overlapping the aorta and repeating at regular intervals. The phase-encode direction for this acquisition is anterior to posterior, and the pattern repeats with a spacing tied to the cardiac cycle, so this is pulsatile flow ghosting from the aorta: the periodic motion of arterial inflow between phase-encode steps mismaps signal along phase, not frequency. The fix is a saturation band placed over the vessel proximal to the imaging slab, or gating the acquisition to the cardiac cycle, not a bandwidth change, because bandwidth only helps chemical shift and noise, which sit along the frequency axis.
memory_hooks: Motion and pulsatile flow ghost along PHASE. Chemical shift is strictly along FREQUENCY. Gibbs truncation ringing is usually worst along PHASE, because that axis often has fewer encoding steps, so raise the phase matrix to reduce it.
TOF is bright because it is unsaturated inflow; the same physics means TOF goes dark whenever flow lies in-plane long enough to get repeatedly hit by RF and saturate.

A traveling or walking saturation band sits on one side of the slab to null the vessel you do not want: proximal placement suppresses arterial signal for a venogram, distal placement suppresses venous signal for an arteriogram.
exam_traps: Aliasing (wraparound) comes from an FOV smaller than the anatomy in the phase direction; it is fixed by enlarging phase FOV or using phase oversampling, not by changing bandwidth.
Susceptibility artifact is worst on GRE and EPI (no 180 degree refocusing pulse to correct field inhomogeneity) and mildest on spin echo.
The zipper artifact runs across the image from stray RF (a door left open, a light left on) and is unrelated to flow or motion.

body.prompt: Ghosting artifact from patient motion or pulsatile flow propagates in which direction?
options: The phase-encode direction
The frequency-encode direction
The slice-select direction
Diagonally, at 45 degrees
body.explain: Motion between successive phase-encode steps corrupts the slowly-sampled phase axis, so ghosts replicate along the phase-encode direction. Swapping phase and frequency directions can move ghosts off the anatomy of interest.

body.prompt: In phase-contrast MRA, choosing a VENC well BELOW the true peak velocity causes:
options: Velocity aliasing with apparent flow reversal
A complete loss of all the vessel signal
A prominent chemical-shift artifact
Increased SNR with no real downside
body.explain: PC encodes velocity as phase; velocities beyond the VENC wrap past plus or minus 180 degrees, so the fastest flow is mismapped and can appear to reverse direction. Setting VENC too high, by contrast, wastes velocity sensitivity.

body.prompt: Time-of-flight MRA makes flowing blood bright because:
options: Inflowing spins stay unsaturated while tissue saturates
Gadolinium is always injected first as a rule
Flowing blood has a very short intrinsic T1
The 180-degree pulse refocuses only moving spins
body.explain: Rapid RF saturates stationary tissue to low signal; blood flowing into the slice has not seen those pulses, so it is fully magnetised and bright, which is flow-related enhancement. In-plane flow saturates and dims, which is the main weakness of TOF.

body.prompt: Chemical-shift misregistration (the fat/water edge shift) appears along the frequency direction and gets WORSE when you:
options: Lower the receiver bandwidth or raise field strength
Raise the receiver bandwidth well above normal
Shorten the repetition time TR sharply
Increase the number of signal averages
body.explain: Fat and water precess at slightly different frequencies; a lower bandwidth assigns fewer Hz per pixel, so that frequency gap maps to more pixels of shift, and the gap in Hz grows with field strength. Raising bandwidth reduces the shift, at an SNR cost.

body.prompt: Fine parallel bright and dark lines running alongside a sharp high-contrast interface (for example cord and CSF) are the hallmark of:
options: Gibbs (truncation) artifact
Chemical-shift artifact
Zipper artifact
Magic-angle artifact
body.explain: Truncating k-space at a sharp edge produces ringing (the Gibbs phenomenon): regularly spaced lines paralleling the boundary. Increasing the matrix (sampling more k-space) narrows and reduces it.

body.prompt: A long-TR, long-TE spin-echo sequence produces which weighting?
options: T2-weighted
T1-weighted
Proton density
Diffusion-weighted
body.explain: Long TR reduces T1 weighting and long TE emphasises T2 decay, so the image is T2-weighted with bright fluid.

body.prompt: Which parameter most directly controls the amount of T2 weighting?
options: TE
TR
TI
Flip angle
body.explain: TE sets how much transverse (T2) decay is sampled before readout, so a longer TE gives heavier T2 weighting.

body.prompt: On a standard T1-weighted brain image, cerebrospinal fluid appears:
options: Dark
Bright
The same as fat
Absent
body.explain: CSF has a long T1, so it recovers little longitudinal magnetisation by the next excitation and stays dark on T1.

body.prompt: STIR is often chosen over spectral (chemical) fat saturation because STIR:
options: Suppresses fat evenly despite an inhomogeneous field
Is always the faster of the two suppression methods
Delivers higher signal-to-noise than spectral fat-sat
Requires no inversion pulse to null the fat signal
body.explain: STIR nulls fat by its T1, which is insensitive to field inhomogeneity, so it works where spectral fat-sat fails.

body.prompt: A proton-density-weighted image is produced by:
options: Long TR and short TE
Short TR and short TE
Long TR and long TE
Short TR and long TE
body.explain: Long TR minimises T1 weighting and short TE minimises T2 weighting, so signal tracks tissue proton density.

body.prompt: Enhancement from gadolinium is best demonstrated on which sequence?
options: Post-contrast T1-weighted images
T2-weighted images without contrast
STIR fat-suppressed images
Diffusion-weighted images
body.explain: Gadolinium shortens T1, so enhancing tissue brightens on T1-weighted images acquired after injection.

body.prompt: Doubling the slice thickness (all else equal) has what effect on SNR?
options: Roughly doubles the SNR
Roughly cuts the SNR in half
Has little effect on the SNR
Roughly quadruples the SNR
body.explain: A thicker slice is a larger voxel holding more spins, so signal and SNR rise roughly in proportion to the thickness.

body.prompt: Which change increases spatial resolution?
options: A smaller FOV at the same matrix
A larger FOV at the same matrix
A thicker slice at the same matrix
More signal averages (higher NEX)
body.explain: Shrinking the FOV while keeping the matrix makes each voxel smaller, which improves resolution but lowers SNR.

body.prompt: A rectangular (reduced phase) FOV shortens scan time by:
options: Acquiring fewer phase-encode steps
Lowering the repetition time TR
Raising the receiver bandwidth
Adding more signal averages
body.explain: Reducing the phase-direction FOV drops the number of phase-encode lines, and scan time scales with that count.

body.prompt: Parallel imaging at an acceleration factor of R=2 mainly:
options: Halves the phase-encode lines to shorten the scan
Doubles the signal-to-noise of the image
Doubles the spatial resolution of the image
Removes essentially all image artifacts
body.explain: Coil sensitivity encoding lets you skip phase lines, cutting scan time by about R, but SNR falls by roughly g times the square root of R.

body.prompt: The main penalty of using a very high receiver bandwidth is:
options: Reduced SNR
Worse chemical shift
A longer minimum TE
Wraparound
body.explain: A wider bandwidth samples the echo faster and admits more noise per pixel, so SNR drops (though chemical shift improves).

body.prompt: Partial-Fourier (half-Fourier) acquisition shortens the scan by:
options: Sampling just over half of k-space by symmetry
Doubling the number of signal averages
Raising the receiver bandwidth substantially
Enlarging the field of view in the phase direction
body.explain: k-space is nearly conjugate-symmetric, so slightly more than half is sampled and the remainder is estimated, at some SNR cost.

body.prompt: The principal hazard of the static magnetic field is:
options: The projectile effect on ferromagnetic objects
Tissue heating from RF energy deposition
Peripheral nerve stimulation from gradients
Acoustic noise from gradient switching
body.explain: The always-on static field can accelerate ferromagnetic objects into the bore with lethal force, so no loose metal is allowed.

body.prompt: Loud acoustic noise during scanning is produced by:
options: Rapid gradient coil switching
The transmitted RF pulses
The static magnetic field
Helium boil-off in the cryostat
body.explain: Gradient coils flex against the static field as they switch, generating the knocking noise that mandates hearing protection.

body.prompt: Peripheral nerve stimulation during fast sequences is caused by:
options: Rapidly switching gradients (dB/dt)
The strong static magnetic field
RF energy heating the tissue
The injected contrast agent
body.explain: Fast-changing gradient fields induce currents that can stimulate peripheral nerves, felt as tingling or twitching.

body.prompt: SAR (specific absorption rate) quantifies:
options: RF power deposited as heat per unit body mass
The gradient slew rate in tesla per metre
The static magnetic field strength
The acoustic noise output of the scanner
body.explain: SAR measures RF energy absorbed as heat, in watts per kilogram, and is limited to prevent excessive patient heating.

body.prompt: During a magnet quench, the immediate life-threatening risk inside the magnet room is:
options: Oxygen displacement if helium fills the room
Electric shock from the magnet windings
A burst of ionising radiation exposure
A ferromagnetic projectile flying in
body.explain: A quench boils off helium; if the vent fails, the cold gas can displace room oxygen, so the room must be evacuated.

body.prompt: Zone IV of an MRI facility refers to:
options: The magnet scanner room itself
The public reception waiting area
The scanner control room
The patient changing area
body.explain: Zone IV is the scanner room, the most restricted zone, entered only after full screening because the field is always on.

body.prompt: A metallic implant of unknown composition and no documentation should be treated as:
options: MR-unsafe until proven otherwise
MR-safe with no restrictions
MR-conditional at any field strength
Low risk and generally acceptable
body.explain: Without documentation you cannot confirm safe conditions, so the conservative and correct approach is to treat it as unsafe.

body.prompt: Non-conditional cardiac pacemakers are dangerous in MRI mainly because the fields can:
options: Alter device function or heat the leads
Permanently demagnetise the battery
Block the RF transmit signal entirely
Erase the device's stored diagnostic logs
body.explain: The static, gradient and RF fields can reprogram or inhibit the device and induce lead-tip heating, risking arrhythmia or burns.

body.prompt: A patient reporting a history of grinding metal who may have an eye fragment needs which study first?
options: Orbital radiographs
Renal ultrasound
Chest CT
No screening
body.explain: Plain orbital radiographs exclude an intra-orbital metallic foreign body that could move in the field and injure the eye.

body.prompt: Before giving gadolinium to a patient with severe renal impairment, the chief concern is:
options: Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis
Contrast-induced nephropathy
Thyroid storm
Acoustic injury
body.explain: Gadolinium retention in severe renal failure is linked to nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, so eGFR is checked first.

body.prompt: The best single measure to reduce motion artifact from an anxious patient is:
options: Clear communication and comfortable immobilisation
Raising the SAR limit to run a faster scan
Applying a motion-correction filter afterward
Increasing the number of averages only
body.explain: A calm, well-supported, well-informed patient holds still, which prevents motion at its source rather than treating it afterward.

body.prompt: Gradient acoustic noise can reach approximately:
options: 100 to 120 dB
40 dB
200 dB
It is not loud
body.explain: Peak gradient noise commonly reaches 100 to 120 dB, loud enough to damage hearing, so protection is required for everyone.

body.prompt: Which patient can most safely receive gadolinium contrast?
options: One with normal renal function and no prior reaction
One with severe chronic kidney disease stage 5
One with a prior gadolinium anaphylaxis reaction
One in the first trimester of a pregnancy
body.explain: Normal renal function and no prior reaction is the low-risk profile; the other three each carry a specific contraindication or caution.

body.prompt: For a sedated or unstable patient monitored inside the bore, the equipment must be:
options: MR-safe or MR-conditional for the field used
Any standard hospital monitor will do
Lead-shielded to block the field
Battery-powered equipment only
body.explain: Only MR-safe or appropriately MR-conditional monitors may enter the magnet room, to avoid projectiles and image or device interference.

body.prompt: A mild contrast reaction with limited hives and itching is usually managed with:
options: Antihistamines and observation
Immediate intramuscular epinephrine
Furosemide
Intubation
body.explain: Isolated urticaria is a mild reaction treated supportively with antihistamines; epinephrine is reserved for true anaphylaxis.

body.prompt: Balanced SSFP (TrueFISP / FIESTA / balanced-FFE) produces contrast that depends on:
options: The T2/T1 ratio, giving bright fluid
Pure T1 relaxation weighting only
The diffusion of water alone
Proton density weighting alone
body.explain: Balanced SSFP preserves transverse magnetisation so contrast tracks the T2/T1 ratio, making fluid bright, useful in cardiac and MRCP imaging.

body.prompt: An inversion-recovery sequence begins with a pulse of:
options: 180 degrees
90 degrees
45 degrees
A gradient only
body.explain: IR starts with a 180-degree inversion pulse; the chosen TI then selects which tissue is nulled (fat in STIR, CSF in FLAIR).

body.prompt: Diffusion weighting is made stronger by:
options: Increasing the diffusion b-value
Increasing the repetition time TR
Decreasing the echo time TE
Adding more signal averages
body.explain: The b-value scales the diffusion-sensitising gradients, so a higher b-value produces heavier diffusion weighting.

body.prompt: A spoiled gradient-echo sequence deliberately destroys residual:
options: Transverse magnetisation for T1 or T2* contrast
Residual longitudinal magnetisation
The transmitted RF excitation pulse
The frequency-encode readout gradient waveform
body.explain: Spoiling dephases leftover transverse magnetisation between TRs so it cannot contribute steady-state signal, yielding clean T1 or T2* contrast.

body.prompt: The sequence underlying most BOLD functional MRI is:
options: Gradient-echo EPI
Conventional spin echo
STIR
Balanced SSFP
body.explain: BOLD fMRI needs fast T2*-sensitive imaging, provided by single-shot gradient-echo EPI acquired repeatedly over time.

body.prompt: The most sensitive sequence for hyperacute ischaemic stroke is:
options: Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI)
Standard T1-weighted imaging
Proton-density weighted imaging
Post-contrast T1-weighted imaging
body.explain: Cytotoxic oedema restricts diffusion within minutes, so DWI shows infarction long before T2 or FLAIR changes appear.

body.prompt: Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) is especially good at detecting:
options: Microhaemorrhages, iron and calcium deposits
Vasogenic oedema around a mass lesion
Subcutaneous and marrow fat signal
Fast-flowing blood in patent vessels
body.explain: SWI exploits T2* susceptibility, so blood products, iron and calcium bloom and become conspicuous even when tiny.

body.prompt: Vasogenic oedema around a tumour is best appreciated as high signal on:
options: T2 or FLAIR
T1-weighted
SWI
Phase contrast
body.explain: Vasogenic oedema is extra extracellular water, which is bright on T2, and FLAIR nulls adjacent CSF to make it stand out.

body.prompt: Enhancement of a lesion after gadolinium indicates:
options: Blood-brain barrier breakdown or a vascular lesion
Dense calcification within the lesion matrix
High lipid or fatty content within the lesion
Rapid arterial blood flow through the region
body.explain: Gadolinium only reaches tissue where the barrier is broken or vascularity is high, so enhancement flags those processes.

body.prompt: Fat within a lesion is confirmed when its signal drops on:
options: Fat-suppressed sequences
Diffusion-weighted imaging
SWI
Phase-contrast imaging
body.explain: If bright T1 signal disappears with fat suppression, the source is fat, distinguishing a lipoma or dermoid from haemorrhage.

body.prompt: A fluid-fluid level inside a lesion most suggests:
options: Haemorrhage or layering of contents by density
A simple CSF-filled cyst with no debris
Dense calcification within the lesion wall
A vascular flow void from fast flow
body.explain: Settling of blood or proteinaceous debris produces a fluid-fluid level, seen in haemorrhagic cysts and some tumours.

body.prompt: Wrap-around (aliasing) artifact is corrected by:
options: Enlarging the FOV or applying phase oversampling
Increasing the receiver bandwidth setting
Shortening the echo time of the sequence
Adding a spectral fat-suppression pulse
body.explain: Aliasing is undersampling of anatomy outside the phase FOV, so enlarging the FOV or oversampling the phase direction removes it.

body.prompt: The dark India-ink outline around organs on opposed-phase imaging results from:
options: Fat and water signal cancelling in border voxels
Bulk patient motion during the acquisition
Susceptibility at soft-tissue interfaces
Aliasing of anatomy from outside the FOV
body.explain: In border voxels containing both fat and water, their signals are out of phase and subtract, drawing a dark outline.

body.prompt: Signal void and geometric distortion around metallic hardware is called:
options: A metal susceptibility artifact
A chemical-shift artifact
A truncation (Gibbs) artifact
An aliasing wraparound artifact
body.explain: Metal disturbs local field homogeneity, dephasing spins and mismapping them, worst on gradient-echo and EPI sequences.

body.prompt: Saturation (sat) bands are applied to:
options: Suppress signal or flow from a chosen region
Raise the overall signal-to-noise ratio
Shorten the repetition time of the scan
Null fat signal across the whole image
body.explain: A sat band pre-saturates spins in a chosen slab so they give no signal, used to remove flow ghosts or unwanted anatomy.

body.prompt: The magic-angle artifact brightens tendons oriented at about:
options: 55 degrees to the main field on short-TE sequences
90 degrees, perpendicular to the main field
0 degrees, parallel to the main field
Any orientation equally, angle-independent
body.explain: At roughly 55 degrees, dipolar interactions are minimised so tendon T2 lengthens and it appears artefactually bright on short-TE images.

body.prompt: Cardiac and respiratory gating are used chiefly to reduce:
options: Motion and pulsation ghosting artifact
Chemical-shift misregistration artifact
Truncation (Gibbs) ringing artifact
Zipper artifact from stray RF signal
body.explain: Synchronising acquisition to the cardiac or respiratory cycle keeps anatomy in a consistent position, suppressing motion ghosts.

body.prompt: Spectral (chemical-shift) fat saturation works by exploiting:
options: The resonance-frequency gap between fat and water
The T1 relaxation difference between them
The greater diffusion rate of fat protons
The physical flow of fat through tissue
body.explain: A frequency-selective pulse saturates fat at its precession frequency, so it needs a homogeneous field to separate the fat and water peaks.

body.prompt: Spectral fat saturation is most likely to fail:
options: Off-isocentre or near metal, in an uneven field
At the exact isocentre of a shimmed bore
In a uniformly well-shimmed homogeneous field
Only when using a very short echo time
body.explain: Field inhomogeneity blurs the fat and water peaks together, so the frequency-selective pulse can no longer target fat cleanly.

body.prompt: STIR suppresses fat by:
options: Setting a short TI to null fat by its T1
Saturating fat at its resonant frequency
Dephasing fat with a spoiler gradient
Using a very long echo time TE
body.explain: STIR is inversion recovery with TI at the null point of fat's T1, which is insensitive to field inhomogeneity, unlike spectral fat-sat.

body.prompt: Why should STIR generally not be combined with gadolinium?
options: Gadolinium shortens tissue T1 near fat's null, hiding it
The gadolinium contrast agent can cause skin burns
It nulls the water signal instead of the fat signal
It roughly doubles the total acquisition time
body.explain: STIR nulls tissue by T1, and gadolinium-shortened tissue can fall near that same null, masking the very enhancement you want to see.

body.prompt: The Dixon technique separates fat and water using:
options: In-phase and opposed-phase echoes (chemical shift)
Two separate acquisitions at different flip angles
Strong diffusion-weighting gradients
A spatially selective saturation band
body.explain: Dixon acquires echoes where fat and water are in and out of phase, then combines them to compute separate water-only and fat-only images.

body.prompt: Water excitation suppresses fat by:
options: Selectively exciting only the water protons
Inverting the fat protons first
Dephasing the water signal with a gradient
Saturating the water resonance
body.explain: A composite RF pulse tips only water into the transverse plane, leaving fat largely unexcited, useful in high-resolution cartilage imaging.

body.prompt: At 1.5 T compared with 3 T, spectral fat saturation is:
options: Harder, the fat-water gap in Hz is smaller
Easier, since the peaks are farther apart
Unaffected, independent of field strength
Impossible to achieve at 1.5 T
body.explain: The chemical-shift separation scales with field strength, so the fat and water peaks are closer together at 1.5 T, making selective saturation harder.

body.prompt: The main reason to suppress fat before or after gadolinium is to:
options: Raise contrast of enhancement and oedema by cutting fat
Shorten the overall repetition time of the scan
Reduce the specific absorption rate to the patient
Prevent aliasing and wraparound in the image
body.explain: Bright fat can hide enhancing lesions and marrow or soft-tissue oedema, so removing it raises the contrast of the findings you care about.

body.prompt: The periphery of k-space predominantly encodes:
options: Fine detail and high-spatial-frequency resolution
The overall image contrast and brightness
The slice selection and slice position
The receiver gain and coil setting
body.explain: High spatial frequencies at the edges of k-space carry edges and fine detail, while the centre carries bulk signal and contrast.

body.prompt: Frequency encoding is performed:
options: During readout, while the frequency gradient is on
Just before the excitation RF pulse is applied
During slice selection only, not readout
After the image has been reconstructed
body.explain: The readout (frequency-encode) gradient is applied while the echo is sampled, mapping position along that axis to signal frequency.

body.prompt: Phase encoding differs from frequency encoding in that it is:
options: Stepped once per TR to fill successive k-space lines
Applied continuously during the entire readout
Never based on a magnetic gradient
Used only in 3D volume imaging
body.explain: Each TR applies a different phase-encode gradient amplitude to fill one k-space line, which is why the phase matrix drives scan time.

body.prompt: The mathematical operation that converts sampled k-space into an image is the:
options: Fourier transform
Laplace transform
Convolution kernel
Hough transform
body.explain: A 2D (or 3D) inverse Fourier transform turns the spatial-frequency (k-space) data into the spatial-domain image.

body.prompt: Aliasing (wraparound) is avoided when sampling satisfies the Nyquist criterion, meaning:
options: The FOV covers the whole object in the phase direction
The echo time TE is kept short enough
The receiver bandwidth is set high enough for it
The flip angle is kept small enough
body.explain: Undersampling anatomy outside the phase FOV violates Nyquist and folds it back; covering the object or oversampling prevents the wrap.

body.prompt: A true 3D acquisition encodes the slice direction by:
options: A second phase-encode gradient along the slab
A thicker slice-select excitation pulse
A longer frequency readout window
Averaging more signal acquisitions
body.explain: 3D imaging phase-encodes through the slab thickness, yielding thin contiguous partitions and high SNR from the whole-volume excitation.

body.prompt: Zero-filling (k-space interpolation) does what?
options: Interpolates to a finer display matrix, no new resolution
Acquires additional real k-space lines during the scan
Raises the true spatial resolution of the final image
Filters out random noise to boost the image SNR
body.explain: Padding k-space with zeros produces a smoother, larger display matrix but adds no new high-frequency data, so real resolution is unchanged.

body.prompt: Centric (low-to-high) k-space ordering is used to:
options: Capture contrast at the moment of peak arterial enhancement
Increase the acquisition matrix without extra scan time
Lower the SAR deposited during long echo train sequences
Suppress fat signal by nulling it at the k-space centre
body.explain: Sampling the k-space centre first locks in contrast at that instant, valuable in dynamic contrast MRA where arterial timing matters.

body.prompt: Clinical superconducting magnets maintain their field because the windings are:
options: Cooled by liquid helium to become superconducting
Built from permanently magnetised alloy blocks
Powered continuously from the mains electricity supply
Cooled by liquid nitrogen alone, with no helium bath
body.explain: Superconducting niobium-titanium coils bathed in liquid helium carry current with no resistance, sustaining a stable high field.

body.prompt: Shimming is performed to:
options: Improve homogeneity of the main magnetic field
Increase the strength of the imaging gradients
Boost the RF transmit power to the body coil
Keep the magnet windings at cryogenic temperature
body.explain: Passive or active shims correct field inhomogeneity, which is essential for spectral fat suppression and artifact-free imaging.

body.prompt: Gradient coils are responsible for:
options: Producing linear field variation used for spatial encoding
Exciting the spins by transmitting the RF pulse
Circulating coolant to keep the bore temperature stable
Detecting the MR signal returning from the patient
body.explain: The x, y and z gradient coils superimpose position-dependent field changes used for slice selection and frequency and phase encoding.

body.prompt: The RF transmit coil primarily:
options: Excites the spins by producing the B1 field
Encodes spatial position along each axis
Removes heat from the superconducting magnet
Shields the receiver from external RF noise
body.explain: The transmit coil delivers the B1 RF pulse that tips magnetisation; receive coils then detect the returning signal.

body.prompt: Phased-array surface coils are used chiefly to:
options: Raise SNR near the coil and enable parallel imaging
Increase the strength of the static magnetic field
Generate the gradients used for spatial encoding
Suppress fat signal near the surface of the body
body.explain: Multiple small elements each see high local SNR and provide the spatial sensitivity information that parallel imaging exploits.

body.prompt: The RF (Faraday) shield around the scanner room prevents:
options: External radiofrequency interference (e.g. zipper artifact)
Leakage of the static fringe field into nearby rooms
Loss of helium boil-off gas from the magnet cryostat
Acoustic noise from gradient switching reaching staff
body.explain: The conductive shield blocks stray external RF from corrupting the received signal, which would otherwise show as zipper or noise bands.

body.prompt: Moving from 1.5 T to 3 T generally increases all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Inherent acoustic quietness of the scanner
SNR
SAR
Chemical-shift and susceptibility effects
body.explain: Higher field raises SNR but also SAR, chemical shift and susceptibility; it does not inherently make the scanner quieter.

body.prompt: The fringe (stray) field outside the bore is the reason for:
options: The 5-gauss line and access restrictions around the magnet
The hearing protection worn during every acquisition
Renal function screening before contrast injection
The water cooling needed by the gradient amplifiers
body.explain: The static fringe field extends beyond the bore; the 5-gauss line marks where it can affect implants and electronics, so access is controlled.

body.prompt: A key advantage of a 3D volumetric acquisition over 2D multislice is:
options: Thin contiguous slices with high SNR that reformat in any plane
A consistently lower SAR regardless of the sequence used
No reliance on gradients for encoding the third dimension
Complete immunity to patient motion during the scan
body.explain: 3D imaging excites the whole slab, giving high SNR, thin gapless partitions and isotropic data that can be reformatted freely.

body.prompt: A maximum-intensity projection (MIP) is used mainly to display:
options: Bright vessels in MR angiography
Dark veins on susceptibility scans
Fat planes on unenhanced T1 images
CSF flow voids in the aqueduct
body.explain: MIP renders the brightest voxel along each ray, ideal for showing the high signal of arteries in a TOF or contrast-enhanced MRA.

body.prompt: Isotropic voxels are desirable because they allow:
options: Multiplanar reformatting in any plane without distortion
Shorter RF pulses and therefore much faster excitation
Diagnostic imaging at much lower field strength
Uniform fat suppression across the whole volume
body.explain: Equal voxel dimensions in all three directions let reformatted planes preserve resolution, so one acquisition serves every viewing angle.

body.prompt: A minimum-intensity projection (MinIP) is best suited to display:
options: Dark structures such as veins on susceptibility imaging
Bright arteries on a time-of-flight angiogram
The bright fat signal on non-suppressed T1 images
An avidly enhancing tumour after gadolinium
body.explain: MinIP keeps the darkest voxel along each ray, which highlights low-signal structures like veins on SWI or air in the airways.

body.prompt: Compared with a 2D acquisition, 3D gradient echo typically offers:
options: Thinner, gapless slices and higher SNR per slice
Larger gaps between the individual slices
Lower in-plane resolution for the same matrix
Images that cannot be reformatted afterwards
body.explain: Because the whole volume is excited and phase-encoded through the slab, 3D yields contiguous thin partitions with strong SNR.

body.prompt: Multiplanar reformation (MPR) requires:
options: A volumetric (3D) dataset
A single 2D slice
A projection radiograph
A k-space centre only
body.explain: Reformatting arbitrary planes needs a full volume of data; a single 2D slice cannot be re-sliced in another orientation.

body.prompt: Partial-volume averaging is worst with:
options: Thick slices
Thin isotropic voxels
A high matrix
A small FOV
body.explain: Thick slices blend signal from structures across the slice, blurring small findings; thinner voxels reduce partial-volume effects.

body.prompt: Cross-talk between adjacent 2D slices is reduced by:
options: Interslice gaps or interleaved slice ordering
Running the sequence at a higher SAR
Increasing the field of view of each slice
Acquiring a larger number of signal averages
body.explain: Imperfect slice profiles let neighbouring slices saturate each other; a gap or interleaving separates their excitation in space or time.

body.prompt: Thin high-resolution heavily T2-weighted images of the internal auditory canals are obtained to evaluate:
options: The vestibulocochlear nerve and acoustic neuroma
The pituitary gland and its microadenomas
The menisci and ligaments of the knee joint
The liver and its focal enhancing lesions
body.explain: Sequences like CISS or FIESTA show the cisternal cranial nerves against bright CSF, screening for a vestibular schwannoma.

body.prompt: The pituitary gland is best assessed with:
options: Thin dynamic post-contrast coronal T1 images
Axial diffusion-weighted images of the brain
Thick-slice sagittal T2 images of the sella
A rotating MIP from a time-of-flight MRA
body.explain: Small microadenomas enhance differently over time, so thin dynamic coronal T1 through the sella is the standard technique.

body.prompt: MR cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) depicts the biliary and pancreatic ducts using:
options: Heavily T2-weighted sequences that make static fluid bright
Dynamic post-contrast T1 imaging of the duct walls
Diffusion-weighted imaging as the sole sequence
Time-of-flight inflow enhancement of the bile ducts
body.explain: MRCP relies on the long T2 of stationary bile and pancreatic fluid, so heavily T2-weighted images show the ducts as bright channels.

body.prompt: The supraspinatus tendon of the rotator cuff is best evaluated on:
options: Oblique coronal images
Axial images alone
Sagittal T1 images alone
A thick-slab MIP image
body.explain: The oblique coronal plane parallels the supraspinatus, showing its full length and any tear to best advantage.

body.prompt: Cardiac cine imaging of wall motion typically uses:
options: ECG-gated balanced SSFP
Single-shot EPI diffusion imaging
A fat-suppressing STIR sequence
Time-of-flight MRA
body.explain: Balanced SSFP gives bright blood-to-myocardium contrast and, with ECG gating, produces the cine loops used to assess function.

body.prompt: On a routine spine MRI, cerebrospinal fluid appears bright (a myelographic effect) on:
options: T2-weighted images
T1-weighted images
STIR of marrow
GRE only
body.explain: CSF has a long T2, so heavily T2-weighted sagittals outline the cord and nerve roots against bright fluid.

body.prompt: Characterising a focal liver lesion relies most on:
options: Multiphase dynamic post-gadolinium T1 imaging
A single unenhanced T2-weighted acquisition
Diffusion-weighted imaging on its own
Time-of-flight angiography of the hepatic artery
body.explain: Arterial, portal-venous and delayed phases show the enhancement pattern that distinguishes haemangioma, FNH, HCC and metastases.

body.prompt: The anterior cruciate ligament of the knee is usually best displayed on:
options: Sagittal (slightly oblique) images
Axial T1 images by themselves
Coronal STIR images by themselves
A thick-slab MIP reconstruction
body.explain: The ACL runs obliquely; a sagittal plane angled along the ligament shows its fibres and any tear most completely.

body.prompt: A routine brain MRI protocol most typically includes:
options: T1, T2, FLAIR and DWI, with contrast T1 as needed
A single T1-weighted series covering the whole brain
Time-of-flight MRA sequences without any other imaging
Diffusion-weighted imaging alone, with no other series
body.explain: This core set covers anatomy, fluid-sensitive pathology, periventricular disease and acute ischaemia, with contrast added when indicated.

body.prompt: For suspected hyperacute stroke, the single indispensable sequence is:
options: Diffusion-weighted imaging with its ADC map
Post-contrast T1 imaging of the whole brain
A proton density series through the brain
Time-of-flight MRA of the intracranial vessels
body.explain: DWI detects the restricted diffusion of cytotoxic oedema within minutes, well before conventional sequences change.

body.prompt: A multiple-sclerosis brain protocol places particular emphasis on:
options: FLAIR, with post-contrast T1 to flag active lesions
Time-of-flight MRA of the circle of Willis
Susceptibility imaging as the main plaque sequence
Post-contrast T2 imaging used instead of FLAIR
body.explain: FLAIR shows periventricular and juxtacortical plaques, and enhancement on post-contrast T1 marks lesions with active barrier breakdown.

body.prompt: Intracranial arteries are most commonly screened without contrast using:
options: 3D time-of-flight MRA
Phase-contrast venography
STIR
MRCP
body.explain: 3D TOF exploits flow-related enhancement of inflowing arterial blood, giving a non-contrast angiogram of the circle of Willis.

body.prompt: To reduce CSF-pulsation ghosting on a spine study, a technologist can:
options: Apply flow compensation, gating or saturation bands
Raise the SAR by using more RF pulses per TR
Shrink the field of view to smaller than the cord
Have the patient remove their hearing protection
body.explain: Pulsatile CSF creates ghosts; flow compensation, cardiac gating and sat bands all reduce the signal or phase errors that cause them.

body.prompt: Contrast-enhanced MRA depends critically on:
options: Timing the acquisition to the arterial phase of the bolus
Choosing a very long repetition time to boost signal
Applying fat suppression to the entire volume
Selecting a high b-value for the diffusion gradients
body.explain: CE-MRA is flow-independent but timing-dependent: the k-space centre must be filled while contrast is in the arteries, before venous return.

body.prompt: A temporal-lobe (seizure) protocol characteristically adds:
options: Thin oblique coronal T2 and FLAIR through the hippocampi
Thick axial slices angled along the AC-PC baseline
Sagittal T1 of the whole brain only
Time-of-flight MRA of the circle of Willis
body.explain: Angled thin coronals perpendicular to the hippocampi reveal mesial temporal sclerosis, the common substrate of temporal-lobe epilepsy.

body.prompt: To reduce susceptibility artifact when imaging around metal hardware, a good strategy is to:
options: Use spin echo with high bandwidth and metal-reduction options
Switch to gradient echo sequences for the whole study
Lower the receiver bandwidth as far as possible
Choose a much longer echo time for every sequence
body.explain: Spin echo refocuses static inhomogeneity, and high bandwidth plus view-angle-tilting methods (MARS/MAVRIC/SEMAC) further shrink metal distortion.

body.prompt: The 5-gauss line marks the boundary beyond which:
options: The fringe field is safe for the public and unscreened devices
The gradient coils automatically switch themselves off
Radiofrequency transmission is completely blocked
The cryogens for the magnet are stored and vented
body.explain: Inside the 5-gauss line the static fringe field can affect pacemakers and electronics, so that contour bounds the controlled access area.

body.prompt: Which item poses the greatest projectile hazard in the scanner room?
options: A steel oxygen cylinder
An aluminium walker
A plastic tray
A titanium hip implant
body.explain: Ferromagnetic steel is strongly attracted and can be pulled into the bore with lethal force; aluminium, plastic and titanium are not ferromagnetic.

body.prompt: The cryogen that keeps the superconducting magnet cold is:
options: Liquid helium
Liquid nitrogen
Liquid oxygen
Carbon dioxide
body.explain: Superconducting coils are immersed in liquid helium near absolute zero; a quench boils this helium off, hence the venting and oxygen concerns.

body.prompt: Metallic-containing tattoos or permanent makeup can occasionally cause:
options: Localised heating or skin irritation
A drop in the static magnetic field
A quench of the superconducting magnet
Failure of the gradient coil system
body.explain: Iron-oxide pigments can absorb RF energy and warm, so patients are warned and the area is monitored, though serious injury is rare.

body.prompt: MRI screening of an inpatient is repeated:
options: Before every examination, since implants and status can change
Only at the patient's very first visit to the department
Once per hospital admission, then kept on file
Only when gadolinium contrast will be administered
body.explain: A patient's devices, surgeries and condition can change between visits, so full screening is repeated before each scan.

body.prompt: A ferromagnetic detection system at the entrance to the scanner room is intended to:
options: Catch ferromagnetic objects before they enter Zone IV
Measure the SAR delivered during each sequence
Detect gadolinium contrast in the patient's blood
Monitor the oxygen level in the scanner room
body.explain: Ferromagnetic detectors add a layer of screening at the Zone III/IV threshold, alerting staff to metal that manual screening missed.

body.prompt: During active scanning, the risk of an RF burn is highest when the patient:
options: Forms a conductive loop (crossed skin contact or looped cable)
Wears foam earplugs throughout the whole examination
Lies exactly at the isocentre of the magnet bore
Holds completely still for the entire acquisition
body.explain: Induced RF currents concentrate in conductive loops, so uncrossing limbs, padding skin contact and straightening cables prevents burns.

body.prompt: Informed consent for contrast administration should document:
options: Risks, benefits and alternatives discussed with the patient
Only the patient's weight and renal laboratory values
Only the expected scan time and appointment details
Nothing at all when the injection is routine
body.explain: Valid consent records that risks, benefits and alternatives were explained and the patient agreed, which is both ethical and medicolegal practice.

body.prompt: A simple aid that helps many claustrophobic patients tolerate the bore is:
options: Prism glasses, a mirror, or feet-first or prone entry
Running the sequences at a higher SAR level
A shorter cable on the call button squeeze ball
Removing the padding from around the head coil
body.explain: Letting the patient see out with prism glasses or a mirror, or entering feet-first or prone, reduces the sense of enclosure.

body.prompt: If contrast extravasates at the injection site, the technologist should:
options: Stop the injection, elevate the limb and apply a compress
Continue the injection and complete the examination
Flush the line forcefully with a bolus of saline
Take no action because extravasation is harmless
body.explain: Stopping, elevating and applying a compress limits swelling; most extravasations are minor but the site is monitored for compartment signs.

body.prompt: Young children who cannot hold still for MRI often require:
options: Sedation or general anaesthesia with full monitoring
A move to a scanner with higher field strength
No special preparation beyond standard screening
Gadolinium contrast for every single examination
body.explain: Motion ruins MRI, so young or uncooperative children are frequently sedated or anaesthetised, with MR-safe monitoring throughout.

body.prompt: Regarding MRI in pregnancy, the generally accepted position is:
options: Non-contrast MRI when indicated; gadolinium only if essential
MRI is absolutely contraindicated at any gestational age
Gadolinium enhanced studies are the preferred approach
Only scanning at 3 tesla is permitted during pregnancy
body.explain: MRI uses no ionising radiation and is used in pregnancy when needed; gadolinium crosses the placenta and is reserved for essential cases.

body.prompt: Before administering moderate sedation, the technologist or team should confirm:
options: NPO status, airway assessment and baseline vital signs
A signed consent form for gadolinium contrast
The exact repetition time of every planned sequence
A normal chest radiograph from the past year
body.explain: Safe sedation requires fasting status, an airway assessment and baseline vitals, with monitoring and reversal agents available.

body.prompt: The squeeze-ball or call device is placed in the patient's hand so that they can:
options: Signal distress and summon the technologist at any time
Adjust the image contrast during the acquisition
Change to the next sequence when they feel ready
Start the scan themselves once they are settled
body.explain: Continuous two-way communication is a core safety measure; the call device lets the patient alert staff immediately if a problem arises.

body.prompt: Lengthening TR while keeping TE short shifts contrast toward:
options: Proton density contrast
Heavier T1 weighting
Heavier T2 weighting
Diffusion weighting
body.explain: A longer TR lets more tissues fully recover, reducing T1 weighting; with a short TE the image approaches proton-density contrast.

body.prompt: The inversion time (TI) used by FLAIR to null CSF is approximately:
options: About 2000 to 2500 ms
Approximately 150 ms
Somewhere near 50 ms
As short as 10 ms
body.explain: FLAIR uses a long TI near the null point of CSF's long T1, so fluid is dark while the image keeps T2 weighting.

body.prompt: On a T2-weighted image, most pathology appears:
