body.explain: The shoulder coronal is angled perpendicular to the glenohumeral joint, while the sagittal is angled parallel to it, so the cuff and labrum are seen in profile.

body.title: Body MRI protocols: liver, MRCP, and abdomen/pelvis coverage
body.html:
Dedicated liver MRI is ordered for suspected hepatocellular carcinoma, cirrhosis surveillance, hemangioma characterization, fatty liver, and hepatitis. The patient lies supine with the liver positioned over the posterior spine coil elements and an anterior phased-array body coil placed on top. Whatever the indication, the prescribed slices must cover the entire liver, from the dome down past the inferior tip. A lesion you cannot see is a lesion you cannot report.

MRCP targets the biliary tree and pancreatic duct in patients with gallstones, pancreatitis, a pancreatic mass, or biliary obstruction. Axial coverage runs from the dome of the liver to below the ampulla of Vater, so a distal common bile duct stone at the ampulla is never cut off the bottom of the stack. The patient is NPO for 4 to 6 hours so the gallbladder is distended and the stomach is empty.

Coverage landmarks separate the abdominal exams on the boards. A screening abdomen and pelvis runs from the top of the liver to below the pubic symphysis, usually as two overlapping packages. A renal mass or screening pelvis protocol runs from the top of the adrenal gland to the pubic symphysis. MR enterography for Crohn disease covers the dome of the liver through the anus, because small bowel and perianal disease can coexist.

Female pelvis MRI evaluates fibroids, endometriosis, adnexal masses and ovarian cysts, cervical pathology, and congenital uterine anomalies. The patient is head first and supine with an anterior phased-array coil over the pelvis, after a fast of about 4 hours. Packages are straight by default; only the small field-of-view high-resolution T2 package is angled, and only when a specific organ is the target.
keypoints: Liver MRI covers the entire liver; core indications are HCC, cirrhosis, hemangioma, fatty liver, and hepatitis
Position the liver over the posterior spine elements with the anterior phased-array body coil on top
MRCP axial coverage: dome of the liver to below the ampulla of Vater, NPO 4 to 6 hours
Screening abdomen/pelvis: top of the liver to below the pubic symphysis, often two overlapping packages; renal mass: top of the adrenal to the symphysis
Enterography covers the dome of the liver through the anus
Female pelvis: head-first supine, anterior phased-array coil, roughly a 4-hour fast; packages are straight by default
body.worked_example: You are setting up an MRCP on a patient with suspected choledocholithiasis. You confirm the patient has been NPO for at least 4 hours so bile fills a distended gallbladder. You place the anterior body coil so the phased-array elements span from above the liver dome to the lower abdomen. Prescribing the axial stack, you start above the dome of the liver and extend below the ampulla of Vater, because the stone you are hunting is most likely impacted in the distal duct. Stopping at the pancreatic head would risk missing exactly the finding the exam was ordered for.
memory_hooks: MRCP goes Dome to Duodenum: the ducts drain down to the ampulla, so cover below it
Screening abdomen/pelvis is Liver to Landing: top of the liver down to the pubic symphysis
Enterography eats everything: dome of the liver all the way through the anus
exam_traps: Stopping MRCP coverage at the pancreatic head instead of extending below the ampulla of Vater
Mixing up renal-mass coverage (top of adrenal to symphysis) with screening abdomen/pelvis (top of liver to symphysis)
Angling female pelvis packages by default; they stay straight unless the small-FOV T2 package is targeting the uterus or cervix

body.title: Body MRI technique: contrast agents, breath-hold vs navigator, MRCP, and orientation
body.html:
Weight-based extracellular gadolinium is the default agent for contrast-enhanced body MRI. Switch to a hepatobiliary contrast agent for focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) and for the living-liver-donor protocol: functioning hepatocytes take the agent up and excrete it into bile, which produces delayed hepatobiliary-phase images. FNH contains functioning hepatocytes, so it retains the agent while most other lesions wash out to darkness.

Respiratory strategy is a protocol decision, not an afterthought. A cooperative patient can breath-hold a 3D T1 gradient echo. A poor breath-holder gets respiratory-triggered or navigator-gated sequences plus single-shot fast spin echo and free-breathing radial 3D T1 gradient echo acquisitions instead of long breath-holds. Quantitative sequences have their own rules: proton density fat fraction (PDFF) quantifies hepatic fat and supports iron and hemochromatosis workups, and it must run before contrast. MR elastography maps liver stiffness; elastography and donor patients fast about 4 hours to reduce bowel motion.

MRCP is heavily T2 weighted, so static bile and pancreatic-duct fluid stay bright while flowing blood and solid tissue go dark. Before the scan the patient swallows a dilute oral agent, water mixed with a small amount of gadolinium, which shortens the T2 of bowel fluid and darkens it so it does not overlie the ducts. This is not IV contrast. Secretin transiently dilates the pancreatic duct and stimulates exocrine output, improving duct visualization and allowing dynamic assessment for chronic pancreatitis, strictures, and obstructing duct stones.

Timing and orientation round out the technique. Routine post-contrast abdominal imaging uses an empiric scan delay of about 30 seconds, but enterography and hematuria or bladder work use a free-breathing dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) acquisition with a short inject delay. In the female pelvis, angle the small field-of-view high-resolution T2 package to the uterus for endometrial cancer and congenital uterine anomalies, and to the cervix for cervical cancer. An antispasmodic (anti-peristaltic) agent can be given to quiet bowel motion.
keypoints: Weight-based extracellular gadolinium is the default; use a hepatobiliary agent for FNH and the living-donor protocol
Poor breath-holder: respiratory-triggered or navigator-gated sequences plus single-shot and free-breathing radial acquisitions
PDFF quantifies fat and supports iron/hemochromatosis workups; it must be acquired pre-contrast. MR elastography maps stiffness
MRCP is heavily T2 weighted; the dilute oral gadolinium drink darkens bowel fluid and is not IV contrast
Routine post-contrast uses an empiric 30 second delay; enterography and hematuria/bladder work use free-breathing DCE with a short inject delay
Angle the small-FOV T2 package to the uterus for endometrial cancer and anomalies, to the cervix for cervical cancer
body.worked_example: A patient arrives for lesion characterization and the report question is whether a 3 cm mass is FNH. You select a hepatobiliary contrast agent rather than the routine extracellular agent, because hepatocyte uptake and biliary excretion give you a delayed hepatobiliary phase. FNH keeps functioning hepatocytes, so it should retain contrast and stay bright on that phase while most other masses go dark. You also confirm the PDFF map is scheduled before injection, since gadolinium would corrupt the fat quantification. The whole protocol hinges on picking the right agent before the needle goes in.
memory_hooks: FNH = Functioning hepatocytes, Needs Hepatobiliary agent
PDFF: Pre-contrast, and Fat fraction is what it measures; the same multi-echo scan supports iron assessment
Uterus for uterine (endometrial) cancer, Cervix for cervical cancer: angle to the organ that has the disease
exam_traps: Crediting IV gadolinium for dark bowel fluid on MRCP; the swallowed dilute oral agent does that by shortening bowel-fluid T2
Choosing routine extracellular gadolinium for an FNH workup; only a hepatobiliary agent gives the delayed hepatobiliary phase
Running PDFF after injection; gadolinium changes the signal, so fat and iron quantification must come pre-contrast

body.prompt: Which clinical scenario is a standard indication for dedicated liver MRI?
options: Surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma in a patient with cirrhosis
Staging of cervical carcinoma before definitive surgical management
Assessment of active small bowel inflammation in Crohn disease
Evaluation of a suspected congenital anomaly of the uterine cavity
body.explain: HCC surveillance in cirrhosis is a core liver MRI indication, along with hemangioma, fatty liver, and hepatitis. The other scenarios call for pelvic MRI or MR enterography instead.

body.prompt: When prescribing slices for a dedicated liver MRI, the imaging volume must:
options: Include the entire liver from the dome to the inferior tip
Cover only the lobe that contains the suspected pathology
Extend from the diaphragm to the pubic symphysis every time
Match the coverage used on the localizer without adjustment
body.explain: Whatever the indication, liver protocols cover the whole organ so no lesion falls outside the stack. Restricting coverage to one lobe risks missing synchronous disease, and extending to the symphysis is a screening abdomen/pelvis, not a liver exam.

body.prompt: For liver MRI with a phased-array body coil, correct patient setup places:
options: The liver over the posterior spine elements with the anterior coil on top
The anterior coil alone in use, since posterior elements add ghosting
The patient prone so the liver falls toward the anterior coil elements
The posterior elements switched off to limit respiratory motion artifact
body.explain: Signal comes from both sides: the patient lies over the posterior spine elements while the anterior phased-array coil covers the abdomen from above. Posterior elements contribute signal, not ghosting, and routine liver imaging is done supine.

body.prompt: Axial coverage for MRCP should extend:
options: From the dome of the liver to below the ampulla of Vater
From the top of the adrenal glands to the pubic symphysis
From the gastroesophageal junction to the aortic bifurcation
From the pancreatic tail to the lower pole of the right kidney
body.explain: MRCP must include the entire biliary tree, so the stack runs from above the liver dome to below the ampulla of Vater where a distal duct stone would sit. Adrenal-to-symphysis coverage belongs to the renal mass protocol.

body.prompt: A screening abdomen and pelvis MRI is typically prescribed as:
options: Two overlapping packages from the top of the liver to below the pubic symphysis
A single package from the diaphragm to the iliac crest with no overlap permitted
Two separate packages from the xiphoid to the umbilicus and umbilicus to the groin
One thick-slab package from the top of the kidneys down to the femoral neck level
body.explain: The screening exam covers the top of the liver to below the pubic symphysis, usually split into two overlapping axial packages so nothing is skipped at the junction. Coverage stopping at the iliac crest omits the pelvis entirely.

body.prompt: Coverage for a renal mass MRI protocol extends:
options: From the top of the adrenal gland to the pubic symphysis
From the dome of the liver through the anus in one package
From the renal hila to the aortic bifurcation with overlap
From the diaphragm to the iliac crest in two thin packages
body.explain: Renal mass and screening pelvis protocols run from the top of the adrenal gland to the pubic symphysis, capturing the adrenal, both kidneys, the ureters, and the bladder. Dome-of-liver-through-anus is the enterography prescription.

body.prompt: MR enterography for Crohn disease should cover:
options: The dome of the liver through the anus
The pylorus to the ileocecal valve only
The top of the kidneys to the symphysis
The stomach through the sigmoid colon
body.explain: Enterography covers the dome of the liver through the anus because Crohn disease can involve any bowel segment and perianal fistulas are common. Stopping at the ileocecal valve or sigmoid would miss perianal disease.

body.prompt: A dedicated female pelvis MRI would most appropriately be ordered for:
options: Characterizing an adnexal mass found on ultrasound
Quantifying hepatic fat fraction and iron deposition
Grading a pancreatic duct stricture after pancreatitis
Following small bowel disease activity in Crohn disease
body.explain: Adnexal masses and ovarian cysts are standard female pelvis indications, together with fibroids, endometriosis, cervical pathology, and congenital uterine anomalies. Fat quantification, duct strictures, and Crohn disease are liver, MRCP, and enterography territory.

body.prompt: Standard positioning for female pelvis MRI is:
options: Head first and supine with an anterior phased-array coil over the pelvis
Feet first and prone with the spine coil alone covering the sacral region
Head first and prone with an endocavitary coil required for every study
Feet first and supine using only the built-in body coil for reception
body.explain: The patient goes in head first and supine with an anterior phased-array coil centered over the pelvis for surface-coil signal. Endocavitary coils are not routine, and the built-in body coil alone sacrifices signal-to-noise.

body.prompt: Before MR elastography of the liver, the patient should:
options: Fast for about 4 hours to reduce bowel motion
Drink a liter of water during the prior hour
Complete a laxative bowel prep the night before
Remain NPO for a full 24 hours before arrival
body.explain: Elastography and living-donor patients fast roughly 4 hours, which quiets bowel motion during the exam. A 24 hour fast is excessive and water loading or laxative preps are not part of the preparation.

body.prompt: For a routine contrast-enhanced liver MRI with no request for hepatobiliary-phase imaging, the standard agent is:
options: Weight-based extracellular gadolinium
A fixed-dose hepatobiliary contrast agent
Dilute oral gadolinium mixed with water
Superparamagnetic iron oxide particles
body.explain: Extracellular gadolinium dosed by patient weight is the default for body MRI. Hepatobiliary agents are reserved for specific indications such as FNH and the living-donor protocol, and the dilute oral mixture is a bowel-darkening drink, not an IV agent.

body.prompt: A liver MRI is ordered to confirm suspected focal nodular hyperplasia. Which contrast choice is most appropriate, and why?
options: A hepatobiliary agent, because hepatocytes take it up and excrete it into bile
Extracellular gadolinium, because FNH never enhances on delayed phase images
No intravenous contrast, because FNH is fully characterized on T2 imaging
An oral dilute gadolinium agent, because it outlines the adjacent bowel loops
body.explain: FNH contains functioning hepatocytes, so a hepatobiliary agent is retained on delayed hepatobiliary-phase images while most other lesions wash out. The same agent choice applies to the living-liver-donor protocol.

body.prompt: A patient cannot sustain a 20 second breath-hold for liver imaging. The best protocol adjustment is to:
options: Use respiratory-triggered or navigator-gated sequences with single-shot and radial acquisitions
Add more signal averages to the breath-hold sequences so ghosting cancels across excitations
Schedule the patient for general anesthesia, since free-breathing imaging is nondiagnostic
Apply cardiac gating to every sequence so acquisition avoids diaphragmatic motion windows
body.explain: Respiratory-triggered or navigator-gated sequences, single-shot fast spin echo, and free-breathing radial 3D T1 gradient echo acquisitions all tolerate free breathing. Averaging within a failed breath-hold does not fix motion, and free-breathing techniques make anesthesia unnecessary.

body.prompt: Proton density fat fraction (PDFF) mapping of the liver should be acquired:
options: Before contrast, to quantify steatosis and support iron assessment
During the arterial phase, when hepatic fat signal peaks transiently
In the hepatobiliary phase, once hepatocyte uptake is fully complete
Only after a positive elastography result has confirmed the fibrosis
body.explain: PDFF is a pre-contrast quantitative sequence used for steatosis and for iron and hemochromatosis workups. Gadolinium alters the signal and would corrupt the measurement, so it never runs after injection.

body.prompt: MR elastography of the liver is performed in order to:
options: Map liver stiffness as a marker of fibrosis
Quantify hepatic fat and iron simultaneously
Time the arterial phase of contrast arrival
Suppress respiratory motion during imaging
body.explain: Elastography propagates mechanical waves through the liver and maps tissue stiffness, which tracks fibrosis. Fat and iron quantification is the job of PDFF, a separate pre-contrast sequence.

body.prompt: Why does MRCP display the biliary tree so conspicuously?
options: Heavy T2 weighting keeps static duct fluid bright while background tissue goes dark
Heavy T1 weighting makes concentrated bile bright before any contrast is injected
Gadolinium excreted into bile raises duct signal on the delayed phase acquisitions
Fat suppression nulls the liver so any remaining signal must come from the ducts
body.explain: MRCP is heavily T2 weighted, so stationary fluid in the bile and pancreatic ducts stays bright while flowing blood and solid tissue lose signal. No IV contrast is needed to make the ducts visible.

body.prompt: Before MRCP the patient swallows water mixed with a small amount of gadolinium. The purpose of this oral agent is to:
options: Shorten the T2 of bowel fluid so it darkens and stops obscuring the ducts
Brighten the stomach and duodenum so the ampulla is easier to identify
Provide enhancement equivalent to IV injection without using a cannula
Distend the small bowel loops so wall thickening can be judged reliably
body.explain: The dilute oral gadolinium shortens the T2 of overlapping bowel fluid, nulling it on the heavily T2-weighted MRCP images so the ducts stand out. It is a negative oral agent, not a substitute for IV contrast.

body.prompt: Secretin is administered during MRCP primarily because it:
options: Transiently dilates the pancreatic duct and improves its visualization
Paralyzes bowel peristalsis for the duration of the whole acquisition
Contracts the gallbladder so cystic duct patency can be demonstrated
Reduces gastric fluid signal that would otherwise overlie the ducts
body.explain: Secretin stimulates pancreatic exocrine output and transiently dilates the pancreatic duct, sharpening duct visualization and allowing dynamic assessment for chronic pancreatitis, strictures, and obstructing stones. Quieting peristalsis is the role of an antispasmodic agent.

body.prompt: Routine post-contrast abdominal imaging begins after an empiric delay of about 30 seconds. Which exam instead uses a free-breathing dynamic (DCE) acquisition with a short inject delay?
options: MR enterography for Crohn disease
MRCP for suspected biliary stones
Screening liver MRI for hemangioma
PDFF mapping for hepatic steatosis
body.explain: Enterography, like hematuria and bladder work, replaces the empiric 30 second delay with a free-breathing DCE injection started shortly after contrast. Liver hemangioma uses breath-hold multiphase empiric-delay imaging, not free-breathing DCE, while MRCP and PDFF are non-contrast techniques.

body.prompt: When setting up a pelvis MRI for known cervical carcinoma, the small field-of-view high-resolution T2 package should be:
options: Obliqued to the axis of the cervix
Obliqued to the endometrial cavity
Left straight axial with no angling
Aligned to the long axis of the vagina
body.explain: The small-FOV T2 package is angled to the cervix for cervical cancer and to the uterus for endometrial cancer and congenital uterine anomalies. All other pelvic packages stay straight by default.

body.title: MRI coils: field coils, RF coil types, and coil selection
body.html:
Every MR system relies on a chain of coils. The main field coil produces the static B0 field. Shim coils carry small correction currents that improve B0 homogeneity across the imaging volume. Gradient coils temporarily vary the field strength with position so signal can be spatially encoded: X along right-left, Y along anterior-posterior, and Z along head-foot. The RF transmit coil produces the B1 field, perpendicular to B0, that tips protons out of alignment, and receive coils detect the returning MR signal.

Coils on the patient side come in three functional types. Transmit-only coils are built into the bore wall; this built-in body coil transmits for surface-coil exams and acts as a T/R coil when used alone. Receive-only surface coils, such as the head/neck, spine, foot/ankle, shoulder, wrist, and body phased arrays, are placed on or around the patient and can be combined with each other. Transmit-receive (T/R) coils, such as a circularly polarized (CP) head coil, a knee coil, or the inherent body coil, need a T/R switch and cannot be combined with any other coil. Because a local T/R coil such as the head or knee coil transmits over a small volume, it carries a lower RF heating risk and is preferred for some implant cases.

Element count and fit drive image quality. More elements concentrate sensitivity and raise SNR over a local region, and arrays support parallel imaging for faster scans and broad coverage; the trade-offs are wrap or aliasing artifact and burn risk from elements and cables. Fill factor describes how much of the coil's sensitive volume the imaged part occupies, so fitting the coil closely to the anatomy raises SNR and image quality.
keypoints: B0 coil makes the static field; shim coils smooth it; gradient coils vary it with position for spatial encoding
Gradient axes: X is right-left, Y is anterior-posterior, Z is head-foot
The RF transmit coil produces B1 perpendicular to B0 to excite protons; receive coils detect the signal
Receive-only surface coils can be combined with each other; a T/R coil (CP head, knee, inherent body) never can
More elements raise local SNR; a close fit raises fill factor and SNR
body.worked_example: A shoulder MRI is ordered on a 3T system. You choose the dedicated shoulder array rather than the flexible body array because it fits the joint closely and raises the fill factor. You seat the coil directly over the humeral head, strap it so it cannot shift, and connect it as a receive-only coil while the body coil in the bore wall transmits. Because it is receive-only, you could add the spine array if the protocol needed more coverage.
memory_hooks: Shim smooths, gradients steer, RF tips, receive listens
T/R travels alone: it can never join a coil combination
Fill the coil with anatomy and you fill the image with signal
exam_traps: Shim coils correct field homogeneity; gradient coils deliberately vary the field. Questions often swap these roles
The CP head coil, knee coil, and inherent body coil are T/R and cannot be combined; receive-only arrays can
More elements mean more local SNR, not automatically fewer artifacts; wrap and burn risk are the array's weak points

body.title: Coil positioning by region: landmarks and setup
body.html:
Landmarks make coil positioning repeatable. For brain exams the head coil is centered at the glabella; when the head coil is used for spine work the landmark moves to the chin. The knee coil markings center at the inferior patella. For a dedicated pelvis exam, the top of the body phased array sits at the iliac crest, and for abdomen, pelvis, or composed exams the array is centered over the abdomen first.

The body phased array works together with the spine coil, so the region of interest must lie within the spine coil's sensitive volume as well as under the anterior array. Extremity coils such as the foot/ankle, shoulder, and wrist coils should fit closely and be padded and strapped to limit motion.

The wrist coil must not be angled more than 54.7 degrees to B0. Beyond that angle the magic angle effect alters T2 decay in tendons and ligaments, raising their signal, most conspicuously on short-TE sequences, and inviting a faulty diagnosis. For multi-station protocols, receive-only coils are combined: head plus spine for brain and spine, foot/ankle plus spine for the Achilles region, neck and chest arrays for the brachial plexus, and peripheral angio arrays plus phased arrays plus spine for runoff studies. A T/R coil cannot be added to any of these combinations.
keypoints: Head coil: center at the glabella for brain, at the chin for spine
Knee coil: center at the inferior patella per the coil markings
Pelvis: top of the body array at the iliac crest; keep the part within the spine coil
Wrist coil: never angle beyond 54.7 degrees or magic angle artifact appears in tendons and ligaments
Combine receive-only coils for brain plus spine, Achilles, brachial plexus, and runoff exams; a T/R coil cannot join
body.worked_example: A pelvis MRI is ordered. You place the patient supine with the spine coil sections under the pelvis, then lay the body phased array so its top edge sits at the iliac crest. You confirm the whole pelvis lies within both the array and the spine coil coverage, strap the array so it cannot slide, and landmark midway between the crest and the symphysis before sending the patient to isocenter.
memory_hooks: Brow for brain, chin for spine
The knee coil kneels to the lower patella
Past 54.7 degrees, tendons lie: keep the wrist flatter than the magic angle
exam_traps: Glabella and chin are both head coil landmarks; which one applies depends on whether the exam is brain or spine
The knee centers at the inferior patella, not the joint line or the superior pole
Magic angle is a positioning error, not a metal artifact; it brightens tendons near 54.7 degrees and can mimic a tear

body.title: RF heating and coil safety: SAR, B1+rms, and burns
body.html:
SAR, the specific absorption rate, is the rate at which the body absorbs RF power, in watts per kilogram (W/kg). It depends on the patient's habitus, weight, and tissue as well as the sequence, so the height and weight entered at registration must be accurate. SAR roughly quadruples when a protocol moves from a 1.5T to a 3T system. Normal operating mode allows less than 2 W/kg whole body and less than 3.2 W/kg to the head; first level controlled mode allows less than 4 W/kg whole body.

When a sequence exceeds the limit, reduce RF deposition: lower the flip angle, choose a low-SAR RF pulse, shorten the turbo or echo train factor, run fewer slices, split the scan into more concatenations, and remove saturation bands that are not needed. Removing blankets and fanning air into the bore keep the patient comfortable while heat builds.

B1+rms is the average effective RF field of the transmit coil for a sequence, in microtesla. Unlike SAR it is patient-independent: it is set by the system, the sequence, and the parameters, and the scanner reports it directly, so it is a more consistent condition to verify than a patient-dependent SAR estimate. Implants often carry a B1+rms condition; a DBS with whole-body eligibility, for example, may require every sequence to stay at or below 2 microtesla, checked before each sequence runs.

Burn prevention is positioning work. Never let the patient touch the bore wall or a bare coil or cable, and pad skin-to-skin contact points such as crossed hands or touching knees with a pad or pillowcase. When a metal implant causes severe artifact or its conditions demand a lower field, a 1.5T system is the better choice, and a T/R coil lowers the heating risk in some implant cases.
keypoints: SAR is the rate of RF power absorption in W/kg; it depends on patient habitus, weight, and the sequence
Normal mode: under 2 W/kg whole body and 3.2 W/kg head; first level: under 4 W/kg whole body
SAR roughly quadruples from a 1.5T to a 3T system
Reduce SAR: lower flip angle, low-SAR pulse, shorter echo train, fewer slices, more concatenations, drop unneeded saturation bands
B1+rms is patient-independent, reported in microtesla, and governs many implant conditions such as a 2 microtesla DBS limit
body.worked_example: A patient with a whole-body eligible DBS arrives for a lumbar spine MRI. You verify the device conditions, which require every sequence to run at or below a B1+rms of 2 microtesla, and confirm the entered height and weight are correct so the SAR estimate is valid. Before starting each sequence you check the reported B1+rms and lower the flip angle on one sequence that reads high. You pad between the patient's hands so no skin touches skin and confirm no part of the patient rests against the bore.
memory_hooks: SAR is watts per kilogram of patient; B1+rms is microtesla of transmit field
1.5 to 3: the field doubles, SAR quadruples
No skin on skin, no patient on bore, no bare cable on patient
exam_traps: B1+rms does not change with patient weight; SAR does. Questions test both the units and the patient dependence
2 W/kg is normal mode whole body, 3.2 W/kg is the head limit, 4 W/kg is first level. Keep the three straight
Adding saturation bands raises SAR; removing unneeded ones lowers it. Comfort measures like fanning do not reduce SAR

body.prompt: After magnet installation, small static field inhomogeneities remain across the imaging volume. Which coils are used to correct them?
options: The shim coils
The gradient coils
The RF transmit coil
The receive arrays
body.explain: Shim coils carry currents that flatten residual variations in the static B0 field, improving homogeneity. Gradient coils vary the field deliberately for spatial encoding, and the RF coils handle excitation and signal reception.

body.prompt: On a cylindrical bore system in standard orientation, the Z gradient varies the magnetic field along which direction?
options: Head to foot, along the long axis of the bore
Right to left, across the width of the patient
Anterior to posterior, from front to back
Obliquely, at 45 degrees to the main field
body.explain: Z runs along the bore and the main field, so the Z gradient encodes the head to foot direction. X covers right to left and Y covers anterior to posterior.

body.prompt: A shoulder array placed on the patient detects signal while the coil built into the bore wall handles excitation. The shoulder array is best described as:
options: A receive-only coil
A transmit-only coil
A transmit-receive coil
A gradient encoding coil
body.explain: Surface arrays such as shoulder, spine, and body coils only detect the MR signal; the transmit coil in the bore wall produces the B1 excitation field. A transmit-receive coil would do both and would need a T/R switch.

body.prompt: A multi-station protocol combines several coils for extended coverage. Which coil cannot be included in the combination?
options: A circularly polarized T/R head coil
A receive-only posterior spine array
A flexible receive-only body array
An anterior receive-only neck array
body.explain: Transmit-receive coils such as the CP head coil, the knee coil, and the inherent body coil switch between transmitting and receiving and cannot be combined with any other coil. Receive-only arrays can be used together freely.

body.prompt: Compared with a coil that has fewer elements, an array with more elements covering the same region provides:
options: Higher SNR concentrated over the region of interest
A more uniform transmit B1 field across the volume
A larger sensitive volume with less aliasing risk
Lower SAR because the RF power is divided further
body.explain: More elements concentrate sensitivity, raising local SNR and supporting parallel imaging. They do not change the transmit field or SAR, and small elements can increase wrap rather than reduce it.

body.prompt: A wrist is scanned inside a large head coil instead of a dedicated wrist coil and the images look noisy. The main reason is:
options: A low fill factor, since the wrist occupies little of the sensitive volume
Magic angle artifact from tendons oriented at 54.7 degrees to the field
Poor B0 homogeneity, since the shim cannot adjust to such a small part
Receiver bandwidth mismatch between the coil size and the field of view
body.explain: Fill factor describes how much of the coil's sensitive volume the imaged part occupies. A small wrist in a large coil leaves most of the volume contributing noise, so SNR drops; a close-fitting coil restores it.

body.prompt: Which of the following is a recognized disadvantage of multichannel receive arrays?
options: Wrap artifact and burn risk from coil elements and cables
Slower acquisitions because parallel imaging is unavailable
Lower SNR near the surface compared with a volume coil
Loss of the ability to angle the slice group obliquely
body.explain: Arrays bring high SNR, speed through parallel imaging, and coverage, but small elements near the skin raise wrap or aliasing risk, and coil elements and cables in contact with the patient are a burn hazard.

body.prompt: For a routine brain exam in a multichannel head coil, the coil and laser landmark should be centered at:
options: The glabella
The tip of the chin
The vertex of the skull
The external auditory meatus
body.explain: Brain exams are centered at the glabella, which places the whole brain in the homogeneous center of the coil. The chin is the head coil landmark for spine exams.

body.prompt: A body phased array is positioned for an abdominal exam. In addition to lying under the anterior array, the imaged region should sit:
options: Within the sensitive volume of the spine coil under the patient
Outside the spine coil so the two arrays do not couple
At the anterior bore wall where the transmit field is strongest
Above the isocenter to keep the gradients within linearity
body.explain: Body array exams use the anterior array together with the posterior spine coil, so the part must sit within the spine coil's coverage. The two receive coils are designed to be combined.

body.prompt: According to the markings on a dedicated knee coil, the knee should be centered at:
options: The inferior patella
The superior patella
The tibial tuberosity
The femoral condyles
body.explain: The knee coil is centered at the inferior margin of the patella, which places the joint line and menisci in the middle of the coil's sensitive volume.

body.prompt: When positioning the body phased array for a dedicated pelvis exam, the top edge of the array is placed:
options: At the iliac crest
At the umbilicus
At the xiphoid process
At the symphysis pubis
body.explain: Placing the top of the array at the iliac crest covers the pelvis from the crest down through the symphysis. Centering higher wastes coverage on the abdomen and can cut off the inferior pelvis.

body.prompt: During a wrist exam the coil and wrist are angled well past 54.7 degrees relative to B0. The resulting risk is:
options: Magic angle artifact raising signal in tendons and ligaments
Chemical shift artifact displacing fat along the frequency axis
Susceptibility artifact distorting the carpal bone cortices
Zipper artifact from RF leakage entering the receive chain
body.explain: Near 54.7 degrees to B0, T2 decay in ordered collagen changes and tendons or ligaments appear falsely bright, which can lead to a faulty diagnosis. Keep the wrist coil angled less than 54.7 degrees.

body.prompt: An Achilles tendon protocol needs combined coverage of the tendon and calf. An appropriate coil combination is:
options: A foot and ankle array combined with the spine coil
A CP transmit-receive knee coil with the spine coil
The inherent body coil combined with a wrist array
A T/R head coil paired with the body phased array
body.explain: Receive-only coils such as the foot and ankle array and the spine coil can be combined for extended coverage. Transmit-receive coils, including the CP head, knee, and inherent body coil, cannot join a combination.

body.prompt: The anterior body phased array is the appropriate primary coil for imaging:
options: The abdomen, pelvis, and chest
The brain and internal auditory canals
The wrist and individual fingers
The cervical spine in isolation
body.explain: The body array covers large torso regions, including abdomen, pelvis, chest, and large habitus exams, working with the spine coil beneath the patient. Dedicated head, wrist, and spine coils serve the other regions better.

body.prompt: Specific absorption rate (SAR) is best defined as:
options: The rate of RF power absorbed by the body, in W/kg
The average transmit field of a sequence, in microtesla
The rate of gradient field switching, in T/s
The total acoustic energy delivered, in decibels
body.explain: SAR is the rate at which RF energy is deposited per kilogram of tissue, expressed in watts per kilogram. It depends on the patient's habitus and weight and on the sequence, which is why the entered height and weight must be accurate.

body.prompt: In normal operating mode, the whole-body SAR limit is:
options: 2 W/kg
4 W/kg
3.2 W/kg
10 W/kg
body.explain: Normal mode allows up to 2 W/kg whole body, with 3.2 W/kg permitted for the head. First level controlled mode extends the whole-body limit to 4 W/kg.

body.prompt: A protocol is moved from a 1.5T system to a 3T system with the same parameters. The SAR is expected to be approximately:
options: Four times higher
Two times higher
About half as high
Roughly unchanged
body.explain: SAR scales roughly with the square of field strength, so doubling B0 from 1.5T to 3T raises SAR about fourfold. This is why SAR limits are reached much sooner at 3T.

body.prompt: A fast spin echo sequence at 3T exceeds the whole-body SAR limit. Which change reduces SAR?
options: Lower the refocusing flip angle
Lengthen the echo train factor
Increase the number of slices
Add another saturation band
body.explain: Reducing the flip angle cuts RF power deposition directly. Longer echo trains, more slices, and extra saturation bands all add RF pulses and raise SAR; low-SAR pulse types and more concatenations also bring it down.

body.prompt: A patient has a DBS system with whole-body eligibility that requires every sequence to stay at or below a B1+rms of 2 microtesla. Which statement about B1+rms is correct?
options: It depends on the sequence, not the entered patient weight
It rises when a larger patient weight is entered at registration
It is expressed in watts per kilogram like whole-body SAR
It cannot be displayed until the sequence has finished running
body.explain: B1+rms is the average effective transmit field for a sequence, reported by the system in microtesla, and is determined by the system, sequence, and parameters rather than the patient. That makes it a precise implant condition to verify before each sequence.

body.prompt: Which positioning step lowers the risk of an RF burn during a lumbar spine exam?
options: Place a pad so the patient's hands do not rest skin to skin
Coil the excess cable into a neat loop on the patient's chest
Tuck the receive coil cable snugly beneath the patient's back
Rest the patient's arms against the bore wall to prevent motion
body.explain: Skin-to-skin contact, such as crossed hands or touching thighs, can complete a conductive loop and cause a burn, so pad those points with a pad or pillowcase. Cables must never be looped or trapped under the patient, and the patient must not touch the bore.

body.title: MR image quality: SNR, scan time, and spatial resolution tradeoffs
body.html:
Every protocol is a negotiation between three things: signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), scan time, and spatial resolution. SNR is the mean signal intensity divided by the standard deviation of the noise. Some of its drivers are fixed once the patient is on the table: field strength, the sequence design, and the tissue itself. The rest are yours at the console: voxel size, TR and TE, the number of signal averages (NEX), receiver bandwidth, and the coil.

Voxel size is the central lever. Signal comes from tissue, so a bigger voxel holds more of it. A larger FOV, a smaller matrix, or a thicker slice all enlarge the voxel and raise SNR; the price is coarser detail. Shrink the voxel for sharper images and the noise floor rises to meet you.

The master tradeoff directions are worth committing to memory:

  • TR up: SNR up, scan time up
  • TE up: SNR down (larger at long TE)
  • Flip angle up (toward the optimum): SNR up
  • NEX up: SNR up, scan time up
  • FOV up: SNR up, resolution down
  • Matrix up: resolution up, SNR down, scan time up
  • Slice thickness up: SNR up, fewer slices needed, resolution down
  • Bandwidth up: SNR down, shorter minimum TE and TR, less chemical shift
  • Parallel imaging: scan time down, SNR down

Receiver bandwidth deserves a second look because it moves in the opposite direction from intuition. Opening the bandwidth samples more noise, so SNR falls, but the readout finishes sooner, which permits shorter TE and TR, and the fat-water chemical shift spans fewer pixels, so that artifact shrinks along with susceptibility effects near metal. Nothing on this list is free: every gain in signal, speed, or sharpness is paid for somewhere else.
keypoints: SNR is the mean signal divided by the standard deviation of the noise
Fixed factors: field strength, sequence design, tissue. Operator factors: voxel size, TR and TE, NEX, receiver bandwidth, coil choice
Bigger voxels (larger FOV, smaller matrix, thicker slices) raise SNR at the cost of resolution
Raising the matrix sharpens the image but lowers SNR and lengthens the scan
Higher receiver bandwidth lowers SNR but reduces chemical shift and allows a shorter minimum TE and TR
body.worked_example: A lumbar spine T2 at 3 mm slices with a 512 matrix comes back grainy. Dropping the matrix to 384 enlarges each pixel and buys back signal, and moving to 4 mm slices adds more. If the radiologist wants the fine detail kept, you add an average instead: same voxel, more signal, and a longer scan is the price you quote before you commit.
memory_hooks: Signal lives in tissue: bigger voxel, brighter image
Bandwidth wider, noise louder, fat shift smaller
Nothing is free: every SNR gain is paid in time or detail
exam_traps: Raising the matrix improves resolution but lowers SNR and lengthens the scan; it never raises SNR
Higher bandwidth lowers SNR, yet it reduces chemical shift and shortens the minimum TE and TR
SNR is defined with the standard deviation of the noise, not the mean of the noise

body.title: Acquisition parameters and k-space: matrix, FOV, NEX, and acceleration
body.html:
Each echo fills one phase-encoding line of k-space, and the scan ends when every line has been collected. That is why, for a conventional non-echo-train sequence, 2D scan time is a simple product: TR times NEX times the number of phase-encoding steps, and a turbo or fast spin echo divides that by its echo train length. Geometry comes from the same parameters. In-plane voxel size is FOV divided by matrix in each direction, and slice thickness supplies the third dimension. The distance factor, the slice gap set as a percent of thickness, trims cross-talk and the number of slices needed, but a generous gap can skip small pathology.

NEX repeats each line and averages the copies. Because the noise is re-sampled along with the signal, doubling NEX raises SNR by only about 40 percent (the square root of two) while the scan time fully doubles; the bonus is smoother motion and pulsatile-flow artifact. Phase resolution shortens a scan differently, by acquiring a reduced percentage of the phase lines and accepting rectangular voxels. FOV phase adjusts coverage in the phase direction without touching resolution, since the line count scales in proportion.

Three techniques change how k-space itself is filled. Partial Fourier acquires part of k-space and calculates the rest from symmetry: faster, with some SNR loss and possible blurring. Oversampling collects data beyond the prescribed FOV so anatomy outside the edge cannot wrap into the image; it adds a little SNR and adds time. Parallel imaging undersamples k-space and unfolds the result using the sensitivity maps of multiple coil elements, cutting scan time by the acceleration factor while lowering SNR by roughly its square root; run it with too small an FOV and an aliasing band can appear in the center of the image.
keypoints: 2D scan time = TR x NEX x number of phase-encoding steps
Doubling NEX gives about 40 percent more SNR (square root of 2) and doubles the scan time
Voxel = FOV/matrix in plane by slice thickness; the distance factor is the slice gap as a percent of thickness
Partial Fourier acquires part of k-space and estimates the rest: faster, lower SNR, possible blurring
Oversampling samples beyond the FOV to prevent wrap; parallel imaging undersamples k-space to save time at an SNR cost
body.worked_example: An abdominal breath-hold sequence runs 24 seconds and the patient cannot manage it. Applying parallel imaging with a factor of two brings it near 12 seconds at a known SNR cost. If that is still too long, reducing phase resolution or narrowing the phase FOV drops more lines, and you check that the smaller FOV still clears the flanks so no wrap folds into the liver.
memory_hooks: Time = TR x NEX x phase steps: only three knobs stretch a 2D scan
NEX pays double for a 40 percent raise
Oversample to stop wrap; undersample (parallel imaging) to save time
exam_traps: Doubling NEX raises SNR about 40 percent (square root of 2), not 100 percent, and it doubles the scan time
Parallel imaging cuts time at the cost of SNR and can leave aliasing in the center of the image if the FOV is too small
FOV phase changes coverage in the phase direction, not resolution

body.title: TR, TE, TI, and flip angle: setting image contrast
body.html:
Two clocks set the contrast of a spin echo image. TR is the time between excitation pulses: it decides how much longitudinal recovery happens before the next pulse, how many slices fit in the acquisition, and how long the scan runs. TE is the time from excitation to the echo, when the data for one phase-encoding line is collected: it decides how much T2 decay is allowed to separate the tissues.

The classic weighting table follows from those two clocks. T1 weighting uses a short TR and a short TE, catching tissues mid-recovery. T2 weighting uses a long TR and a long TE, letting recovery finish and decay do the talking. Proton density uses a long TR with a short TE, silencing both relaxation effects so proton content carries the contrast. Inversion recovery adds a third clock, TI: FLAIR pairs a long TR and long TE with a long TI so CSF crosses its null at excitation, while STIR uses a short TI to catch fat at its null.

The flip angle is the excitation angle that tips magnetization away from B0. For any given TR and tissue there is one angle that yields the most steady-state signal, the Ernst angle. Sequence families keep to characteristic ranges: spin echo and turbo spin echo use a 90 degree excitation with 180 degree refocusing pulses, gradient echo excites below 90 degrees so its short TRs still leave usable longitudinal magnetization, and inversion recovery opens with a 180 degree inversion followed by a 90.
keypoints: T1: short TR, short TE. T2: long TR, long TE. PD: long TR, short TE
FLAIR: long TR and TE with a long TI to null CSF. STIR: short TI to null fat
TR sets slice count and scan time; TE sets how much T2 decay shapes the contrast
The Ernst angle is the flip angle that gives maximum SNR for a given TR
Spin and turbo spin echo use 90 then 180 degree pulses; gradient echo stays under 90; inversion recovery starts with a 180 then a 90
body.worked_example: A brain FLAIR comes back with CSF that is not fully dark and the periventricular lesions are hard to separate from the ventricles. Checking the protocol, the TI was left near the short value used for fat nulling. Restoring the long TI appropriate for CSF at that field strength nulls the fluid, and the lesions stand out against dark ventricles again.
memory_hooks: T1 short and short, T2 long and long, PD long TR with short TE
TI targets: short TI kills fat (STIR), long TI kills CSF (FLAIR)
TR grows slices and time; TE grows T2 contrast
exam_traps: PD pairs a long TR with a short TE; choosing a long TE turns the image into T2 weighting
FLAIR and STIR both null a tissue with TI, but FLAIR uses a long TI for CSF and STIR uses a short TI for fat
Gradient echo excites below 90 degrees; spin echo families use 90 and 180 degree pulses

body.prompt: How is the signal-to-noise ratio of an MR image defined?
options: Mean signal intensity divided by the standard deviation of the noise
Peak signal intensity divided by the mean intensity of the background
Mean signal intensity multiplied by the standard deviation of the noise
Total signal in the image divided by the number of background pixels
body.explain: SNR compares the average signal to the spread of the noise, measured as its standard deviation. Dividing by a pixel count or a mean background value is not how noise is quantified.

body.prompt: Which factor affecting SNR is fixed for a given scanner and cannot be adjusted at the console?
options: The static field strength of the magnet
The number of signal averages acquired
The receiver bandwidth of the readout
The slice thickness of the acquisition
body.explain: Field strength, sequence design, and the tissue itself are fixed. Averages, bandwidth, slice thickness, and the rest of the voxel geometry are operator choices.

body.prompt: With all other parameters unchanged, increasing TR has what effect?
options: SNR rises and scan time gets longer
SNR rises and scan time gets shorter
SNR falls and scan time gets longer
SNR falls and scan time gets shorter
body.explain: A longer TR allows more longitudinal recovery before each excitation, so signal rises, and since 2D scan time is TR times NEX times phase steps, the scan lengthens with it.

body.prompt: The matrix is raised from 256 to 512 with the FOV held constant. What happens?
options: Resolution improves, SNR drops, scan lengthens
Resolution improves, SNR rises, scan lengthens
Resolution worsens, SNR rises, scan shortens
Resolution improves, SNR drops, scan shortens
body.explain: Smaller in-plane pixels sharpen detail but each holds less signal, and the extra phase-encoding steps add time. A higher matrix never raises SNR at a fixed FOV.

body.prompt: Raising the receiver bandwidth has what effect on the image?
options: Lower SNR with less chemical shift artifact
Higher SNR with less chemical shift artifact
Lower SNR with more chemical shift artifact
Higher SNR with more chemical shift artifact
body.explain: A wider bandwidth samples more noise, so SNR falls, but the fat-water shift spans fewer pixels, so chemical shift artifact shrinks. It also permits a shorter minimum TE and TR.

body.prompt: Which change enlarges the voxels and therefore raises SNR?
options: Making the slices thicker at a fixed FOV and matrix
Raising the matrix while the FOV stays the same
Shrinking the FOV while the matrix stays the same
Making the slices thinner at a fixed FOV and matrix
body.explain: Voxel volume is FOV over matrix in plane times slice thickness, so a thicker slice means more tissue per voxel and more signal. A higher matrix or a smaller FOV shrinks the voxel and costs SNR.

body.prompt: What tradeoff comes with choosing thicker slices?
options: More signal but less detail through the slice
More signal and more detail through the slice
Less signal but more detail through the slice
Less signal and less detail through the slice
body.explain: Thick slices average more tissue, raising SNR and covering the anatomy with fewer slices, but small structures within the slice blur together through partial volume.

body.prompt: Besides reducing chemical shift, what does a higher receiver bandwidth make possible?
options: A shorter minimum TE and TR
A higher SNR per acquisition
A smaller acquisition matrix
A wider fat-water pixel shift
body.explain: Faster sampling shortens the readout, so echoes can be placed earlier and TR can come down. SNR falls, not rises, when the bandwidth is widened.

body.prompt: For a standard 2D spin echo acquisition, scan time equals which product?
options: TR times NEX times the number of phase-encoding steps
TE times NEX times the number of phase-encoding steps
TR times NEX times the number of frequency-encode steps
TR times TE times the number of slices in the stack
body.explain: One phase-encoding line is filled per TR per average, so time scales with TR, NEX, and the phase steps. Frequency-encoding points are all sampled within a single readout and add no time.

body.prompt: Doubling the number of signal averages (NEX) produces which result?
options: About 40 percent more SNR and twice the scan time
Twice the SNR and twice the scan time in return
About 40 percent more SNR at the same scan time
Twice the SNR with only a small scan time penalty
body.explain: Averaging re-samples the noise along with the signal, so SNR grows only with the square root of NEX, about 1.4 times for a doubling, while the time cost is the full factor of two. Extra averages also smooth motion and flow artifact.

body.prompt: What sets the in-plane dimensions of a voxel?
options: The FOV divided by the matrix in each direction
The TR and TE chosen for the pulse sequence
The receiver bandwidth and number of averages
The slice gap as a percentage of the thickness
body.explain: Pixel size is FOV over matrix along frequency and phase, and slice thickness supplies the third dimension. TR, TE, bandwidth, and averages change signal and time, not geometry.

body.prompt: Setting phase resolution to 70 percent has what effect?
options: The scan shortens and the voxels become rectangular
The scan shortens and the voxels become smaller
The scan lengthens and the voxels become rectangular
The scan shortens and every slice becomes thicker
body.explain: Fewer phase-encoding lines are acquired, which cuts time, and the phase pixel dimension grows, giving rectangular voxels with mildly reduced sharpness in that direction.

body.prompt: How does partial Fourier shorten an acquisition?
options: It samples only part of k-space and estimates the rest
It samples all of k-space twice and averages the copies
It samples extra lines of k-space beyond the chosen FOV
It skips the center of k-space where contrast is encoded
body.explain: Partial Fourier exploits k-space symmetry, acquiring a bit more than half the lines and calculating the remainder, at the cost of some SNR and possible blurring. The center is always kept because it carries the contrast.

body.prompt: What is the purpose of phase oversampling?
options: To stop wraparound by sampling beyond the FOV
To shorten the scan by sampling fewer phase lines
To sharpen the image by sampling finer detail
To lessen chemical shift by widening the bandwidth
body.explain: Extra data collected outside the prescribed FOV keeps anatomy beyond the edge from folding into the image. It adds a little SNR but lengthens the scan.

body.prompt: A parallel imaging factor of two has which combined effect?
options: Scan time is about halved and SNR is reduced
Scan time is about halved and SNR is increased
Scan time is doubled and SNR is reduced too
Scan time is about halved and SNR is unchanged
body.explain: Skipping k-space lines and unfolding with coil sensitivities cuts the time, but SNR falls by roughly the square root of the factor, and a too-small FOV can leave an aliasing band in the center of the image.

body.prompt: Increasing the phase FOV changes the image how?
options: More coverage along phase with resolution unchanged
More coverage along phase with coarser resolution
Shorter scan time with the coverage left unchanged
Finer resolution with the coverage left unchanged
body.explain: Phase FOV adds or trims coverage in the phase direction while pixel size stays the same, because the line count scales in proportion. Scan time and SNR rise when it grows.

body.prompt: Which statement correctly pairs TR and TE with their roles?
options: TR is the time between excitations; TE is the time to the echo
TR is the time to the echo; TE is the time between excitations
TR is the readout duration; TE is the delay after inversion
TR is the delay after inversion; TE is the readout duration
body.explain: TR spaces the excitation pulses and governs slice count and scan time; TE is when the echo is collected and strongly shapes the contrast.

body.prompt: Which TR and TE combination produces T1 weighting on spin echo?
options: Short TR with a short TE
Long TR with a long TE
Long TR with a short TE
Short TR with a long TE
body.explain: A short TR catches tissues at different points of longitudinal recovery, and a short TE reads out before much T2 decay mixes in. Long TR with long TE gives T2 weighting instead.

body.prompt: A sequence uses a long TR and a long TE, and fluid appears bright. The weighting is:
options: T2 weighting
T1 weighting
Proton density
T2 star weighting
body.explain: The long TR removes T1 differences and the long TE lets T2 decay separate the tissues, so slow-decaying fluid stays bright. PD would pair the long TR with a short TE.

body.prompt: Proton density weighting calls for which parameter pair?
options: Long TR with a short TE
Long TR with a long TE
Short TR with a short TE
Short TR with a long TE
body.explain: The long TR removes T1 effects and the short TE cuts off T2 effects, leaving proton content as the main source of contrast. The classic trap is picking a long TE, which pushes the image toward T2.

body.prompt: In a FLAIR sequence, the long inversion time is chosen to:
options: Null the signal from CSF
Null the signal from fat
Boost the signal from CSF
Boost the signal from fat
body.explain: The 180 degree inversion is timed so CSF crosses its null at excitation, which makes periventricular lesions easier to see. Fat nulling uses the short TI of STIR.

body.prompt: How does a STIR sequence remove the fat signal?
options: With a short TI timed to the recovery of fat
With a long TI timed to the recovery of fat
With a saturation pulse at the fat frequency
With a wider receiver bandwidth at readout
body.explain: Fat has a short T1, so a short inversion time catches it at its null point. A frequency-selective saturation pulse is a different fat suppression method, not STIR.

body.prompt: The Ernst angle is best described as:
options: The flip angle giving the most signal for a given TR
The flip angle giving the most T2 weighting at any TR
The refocusing angle used in every spin echo train
The angle at which fat and water signals cancel out
body.explain: For a chosen TR and tissue T1 there is one excitation angle that maximizes the steady-state signal, and that is the Ernst angle. It matters most in short-TR gradient echo imaging.

body.prompt: Which sequence family runs its excitation flip angle below 90 degrees?
options: Gradient echo
Conventional spin echo
Turbo spin echo
Inversion recovery
body.explain: Gradient echo uses partial flip angles so its short TRs still leave usable longitudinal magnetization. Spin echo families use 90 and 180 degree pulses, and inversion recovery opens with a 180 followed by a 90.

body.title: Making an MR signal: protons, B0, Larmor, and resonance
body.html:
Clinical MRI images the hydrogen nucleus (1H), a single proton found in abundance in water and fat. A proton is a spinning charged particle, and a moving charge creates a magnetic field, so each proton behaves like a tiny bar magnet. Outside the scanner these tiny magnets point in random directions and cancel out.

Inside the bore, the static field B0 forces each proton into one of two states: parallel (low energy) or anti-parallel (high energy). A slight majority sits in the low-energy parallel state, and that small excess adds up to the net magnetization vector (NMV) pointing along B0, the z axis. This longitudinal magnetization cannot be measured directly; it has to be tipped into the transverse plane before it can give a signal.

The protons do not sit still. Each one precesses about B0 like a wobbling top, at the Larmor frequency: fo = gamma x B0. Gamma, the gyromagnetic ratio, is 42.58 MHz/T for hydrogen, so protons precess at about 63.9 MHz at 1.5T and about 127.7 MHz at 3T. Higher field means faster precession.

To tip the NMV, a radiofrequency pulse (B1) is applied perpendicular to B0 at (or very near) the Larmor frequency. Because the RF matches the protons' own precession rate, energy transfers by resonance and the NMV rotates toward the transverse plane. RF at the wrong frequency transfers almost no energy. Once the pulse ends, the rotating transverse magnetization sweeps past the receive coil and induces a small current in it (Faraday induction): that current is the MR signal.
keypoints: Hydrogen (1H) is the imaged nucleus: a spinning charged proton acts like a tiny magnet.
In B0, a slight excess of protons aligns parallel (low energy); the excess sums to the NMV along the z axis.
Protons precess at the Larmor frequency: fo = gamma x B0, with gamma = 42.58 MHz/T for hydrogen (about 63.9 MHz at 1.5T, 127.7 MHz at 3T).
The RF pulse (B1) must be perpendicular to B0 and at the Larmor frequency; resonance is what lets energy transfer and tip the NMV.
Only rotating transverse magnetization induces a current in the receive coil; longitudinal magnetization gives no measurable signal.
body.worked_example: During prescan on a 3T system the scanner searches for the center frequency and settles near 127.7 MHz. The same patient scanned last week on the department's 1.5T magnet ran near 63.9 MHz. Nothing about the patient changed: fo = gamma x B0, so doubling the field doubles the precession frequency, and the transmitter must follow it exactly or the excitation pulse will not resonate with the spins.
memory_hooks: Larmor ladder: 42.58 per tesla, so roughly 64 at 1.5T and 128 at 3T.
No resonance, no signal: the RF must match the spins' own precession frequency.
The coil is deaf to the z axis: signal only comes from magnetization rotating in the transverse plane.
exam_traps: Gamma for hydrogen is 42.58 MHz/T, so the Larmor frequency scales with field strength: 63.9 MHz at 1.5T and 127.7 MHz at 3T.
B1 must be applied perpendicular to B0 and at (near) the Larmor frequency; off-resonance RF does not transfer energy.
Longitudinal magnetization along B0 cannot be measured directly; it must be tipped into the transverse plane first.

body.title: Relaxation: T1 spin-lattice and T2 spin-spin
body.html:
After the RF pulse ends, the tipped magnetization returns to equilibrium by two separate processes that run at the same time. T1 relaxation is the recovery of longitudinal magnetization along B0. It is called spin-lattice relaxation because the protons hand their absorbed RF energy back to the surrounding molecular environment, the lattice, as heat. T1 is defined as the time for a tissue to recover 63% of its longitudinal magnetization.

How fast that hand-off works depends on how the lattice molecules move. Energy transfers efficiently only when the molecular tumbling rate is close to the Larmor frequency. Free water is made of small molecules that tumble far too fast, so the transfer is poor and free water has a long T1. Fat's carbon-bond structure tumbles near the proton's Larmor frequency, transfers energy efficiently, and so has a short T1.

T2 relaxation is the decay of transverse magnetization. It is called spin-spin relaxation because each proton sits in a slightly different local field created by its neighbours, so the spins precess at slightly different rates and drift out of phase. As phase coherence is lost, the net transverse magnetization shrinks. T2 is the time for the transverse magnetization to fall to 37% of its starting value.

For any given tissue T1 is always longer than T2: typical soft-tissue T1 values run about 300 to 2000 ms while T2 values run about 30 to 150 ms, and free water such as CSF runs longer than both. Water, and most pathology because of its raised water content, has a long T1 and a long T2. Fat has a short T1 and a short T2.
keypoints: T1 = longitudinal (spin-lattice) relaxation: energy is released as heat to the lattice; T1 is the time to recover 63% of longitudinal magnetization.
T1 efficiency depends on molecular motion near the Larmor frequency: free water tumbles too fast (long T1), fat tumbles near it (short T1).
T2 = transverse (spin-spin) relaxation: neighbouring spins' local fields cause dephasing; T2 is the time to fall to 37% of the initial transverse magnetization.
T1 is always longer than T2 in a given tissue (typical soft tissue T1 about 300-2000 ms, T2 about 30-150 ms; free water runs longer).
Water and most pathology: long T1 and long T2. Fat: short T1 and short T2.
body.worked_example: Right after an excitation pulse, think about CSF and scalp fat in the same head. The fat protons hand their energy to a lattice that tumbles near the Larmor frequency, so fat's longitudinal magnetization is largely back within a few hundred milliseconds. CSF is nearly pure free water: its tiny fast molecules accept energy poorly, so its recovery drags on for seconds. That difference in energy hand-off, not any scanner setting, is why the two tissues recover at such different rates.
memory_hooks: 1 lattice, 2 spins: T1 is spin-LATTICE (longitudinal), T2 is spin-SPIN (transverse).
63 up, 37 left: T1 marks 63% recovered, T2 marks 37% remaining.
Water is a bad listener: it tumbles too fast to catch the Larmor beat, so its T1 is long.
exam_traps: T1 is the time to 63% recovery, not full recovery; T2 is the time to 37% remaining, not zero.
T1 is always longer than T2 for a given tissue; they never swap order.
Free water has a LONG T1: its small fast molecules transfer energy poorly at the Larmor frequency.

body.title: Dephasing, T2 vs T2*, and the spin-echo refocusing pulse
body.html:
Once the RF pulse switches off, the spins in the transverse plane start to fan out. Two things drive this dephasing. The first is the true tissue process: spin-spin interactions, where each proton feels slightly different local fields from its neighbours. That alone would make the signal decay with the tissue's T2. The second is the magnet itself: no main field is perfectly uniform, so spins in slightly stronger regions precess faster than spins in slightly weaker ones.

Add the two together and the free induction decay dies away faster than true T2. This combined, faster decay is T2*. T2* is always shorter than T2 because it includes everything T2 does plus the external field inhomogeneity. Left alone, the signal would be gone before a useful echo could be sampled.

The spin-echo sequence rescues it with a 180 degree refocusing pulse. Picture runners on a track: after the 90 degree pulse they all start together, then the fast ones pull ahead. The 180 flips everyone over, so the fast spins now sit behind and the slow spins sit ahead. Precessing at their same rates, the fast ones catch up and all the spins come back into phase, forming an echo at the echo time TE. For the rephasing to land exactly at TE, the 180 must be applied at TE/2.

This trick only repairs the dephasing caused by the static field inhomogeneity, because that error is the same before and after the flip. The random spin-spin dephasing is not reversible, so the echo amplitude still decays with true T2. A gradient-echo sequence has no 180 pulse, so it cannot recover the inhomogeneity losses and its signal decays with T2*.
keypoints: Transverse dephasing has two sources: true spin-spin interactions (T2) and main field inhomogeneity.
T2* combines both sources, so T2* decay is always faster (shorter) than T2 decay.
The spin-echo 180 degree pulse flips the spins so fast ones fall behind and catch up, rephasing into an echo at TE.
The 180 degree refocusing pulse is applied at TE/2 so the echo forms exactly at TE.
Spin echo recovers the static field inhomogeneity dephasing (the part that makes T2* shorter than T2); true T2 decay remains, and gradient echo recovers neither.
body.worked_example: A patient with fixed dental braces needs a brain scan. On the gradient-echo localizer the frontal region shows large signal voids: the metal distorts the local field, spins dephase rapidly, and with no refocusing pulse the signal decays at the very short local T2*. The fast spin-echo series looks far cleaner through the same region, because each 180 degree pulse rephases the dephasing caused by that static distortion. The braces did not change; the sequence's ability to refocus static inhomogeneity did.
memory_hooks: The star burns out faster: T2* is always shorter than T2.
Turn the runners around at half time: the 180 sits at TE/2 so everyone finishes together at TE.
Spin echo forgives the magnet's flaws; gradient echo has to live with them.
exam_traps: T2* is shorter than T2 because it adds external field inhomogeneity on top of spin-spin dephasing.
The refocusing pulse is 180 degrees and sits at TE/2, not at TE.
Spin echo recovers the static field inhomogeneity dephasing (not true T2); gradient echo does not.

body.prompt: Which nucleus is the source of the signal in routine clinical MRI?
options: Hydrogen-1
Carbon-13
Sodium-23
Phosphorus-31
body.explain: Clinical MRI images hydrogen (1H) because it is a single proton present in huge quantities in water and fat. The other nuclei are MR-active but far too scarce for routine imaging.

body.prompt: Why does a hydrogen proton behave like a tiny bar magnet?
options: It is a spinning electric charge
It carries a net negative charge
It absorbs the static field energy
It is heavier than other nuclei
body.explain: A moving charge creates a magnetic field, so the spinning positively charged proton has a magnetic moment. Mass and energy absorption have nothing to do with it, and the proton's charge is positive, not negative.

body.prompt: The net magnetization vector (NMV) forms along B0 because:
options: A small excess of protons occupies the parallel state
All protons align parallel to the main magnetic field
Half the protons stop precessing inside the magnet bore
Anti-parallel protons outnumber the parallel population
body.explain: Only a slight majority of protons takes the low-energy parallel state; that small excess sums to the NMV. If all protons aligned parallel the NMV would be enormous, and the anti-parallel state is the less populated one.

body.prompt: In a magnetic field, the parallel and anti-parallel proton states differ in that:
options: Parallel is lower energy and slightly more populated
Parallel is higher energy and slightly more populated
Anti-parallel is lower energy and holds most protons
Both states are equal in energy and in population
body.explain: Alignment with B0 is the low-energy state and a slight majority of protons occupies it. If the two populations were equal there would be no net magnetization at all.

body.prompt: According to the Larmor equation, the precession frequency of a proton equals:
options: Gyromagnetic ratio multiplied by field strength
Field strength divided by gyromagnetic ratio
Gyromagnetic ratio divided by field strength
Field strength squared times a fixed constant
body.explain: The Larmor equation is fo = gamma x B0, a simple product, so frequency rises in direct proportion to field strength. The divided and squared forms would not give the observed linear scaling.

body.prompt: The gyromagnetic ratio of hydrogen is:
options: 42.58 MHz/T
21.29 MHz/T
63.87 MHz/T
127.7 MHz/T
body.explain: Gamma for hydrogen is 42.58 MHz per tesla. 63.87 and 127.7 MHz are the Larmor frequencies at 1.5T and 3T, not the gyromagnetic ratio itself.

body.prompt: For an RF pulse to tip the net magnetization away from B0, it must be:
options: At the Larmor frequency, applied perpendicular to B0
At any frequency, as long as its amplitude is large
At half the Larmor frequency, applied parallel to B0
At twice the Larmor frequency, applied along the z axis
body.explain: Energy transfers by resonance only when B1 matches the spins' precession frequency and is applied perpendicular to B0. Off-resonance RF transfers almost no energy no matter how strong it is.

body.prompt: What actually induces the MR signal in the receive coil?
options: Transverse magnetization rotating past the coil
Longitudinal magnetization resting along the z axis
Heat released to the lattice during T1 recovery
Static gradient fields applied during the readout
body.explain: A changing magnetic field induces a current (Faraday induction), and only the rotating transverse magnetization provides one at the coil. Magnetization sitting still along B0 induces nothing.

body.prompt: T1 relaxation is also known as:
options: Spin-lattice relaxation
Spin-spin relaxation
Free induction decay
Susceptibility decay
body.explain: T1 is spin-lattice relaxation: protons return energy to the surrounding molecular lattice as longitudinal magnetization recovers. Spin-spin relaxation is T2, the transverse process.

body.prompt: During T1 relaxation, the energy the protons absorbed from the RF pulse is:
options: Released as heat to the surrounding lattice
Exchanged only between neighbouring protons
Stored permanently in the transverse plane
Returned to the main static field windings
body.explain: Spin-lattice relaxation means the energy leaves the spin system as heat given to the molecular environment. Energy swapped only between neighbouring spins describes T2, which changes phase, not longitudinal recovery.

body.prompt: T1 is defined as the time for a tissue to:
options: Recover 63% of its longitudinal magnetization
Recover all of its longitudinal magnetization
Lose 63% of its transverse phase coherence
Recover half of its longitudinal magnetization
body.explain: T1 marks 63% recovery of longitudinal magnetization, not complete recovery. Full recovery takes roughly five T1 periods.

body.prompt: T2 is defined as the time for the transverse magnetization to:
options: Decay to 37% of its initial value
Decay completely to zero signal
Decay to 63% of its initial value
Recover 37% of its initial value
body.explain: T2 is the time constant at which 37% of the transverse magnetization remains. It is a decay toward zero, not a recovery, and it does not mean the signal has fully disappeared.

body.prompt: Free water has a long T1 because its molecules:
options: Are small and tumble too fast to transfer energy well
Are large and tumble too slowly to absorb any energy
Are bound so tightly that they cannot move or rotate
Are charged and repel the energy of the excited spins
body.explain: Energy transfer to the lattice is efficient only when molecular motion is near the Larmor frequency. Free water's small molecules tumble far faster than that, so the hand-off is poor and T1 is long.

body.prompt: For any single tissue, how do T1 and T2 compare?
options: T1 is always longer than T2
T2 is always longer than T1
T1 and T2 are always equal
Either one can be the longer
body.explain: Transverse coherence is always lost faster than longitudinal magnetization recovers, so T1 (about 300-2000 ms) always exceeds T2 (about 30-150 ms) in the same tissue.

body.prompt: Which pairing of relaxation times is correct?
options: Water: long T1, long T2; fat: short T1, short T2
Water: short T1, short T2; fat: long T1, long T2
Water: long T1, short T2; fat: short T1, long T2
Water: short T1, long T2; fat: long T1, short T2
body.explain: Water relaxes slowly by both mechanisms, so both its times are long; fat transfers energy efficiently and dephases quickly, so both its times are short. The times travel together for these tissues, they do not split.

body.prompt: Most pathology tends to show a long T2 because diseased tissue usually has:
options: More free water content
More fat cell content
Fewer hydrogen protons
Denser bound proteins
body.explain: Edema and most lesions raise the free water content of tissue, and water carries long relaxation times, so pathology inherits a long T2. Extra fat or dense protein binding would shorten the times instead.

body.prompt: After the RF pulse ends, the transverse magnetization dephases because of:
options: Spin-spin interactions plus main field inhomogeneity
Lattice energy transfer plus receive coil resistance
Gradient coil heating plus chemical fat saturation
Proton density variation plus transmit gain drift
body.explain: Dephasing comes from the local fields of neighbouring spins (true T2) plus the imperfect uniformity of the main field. Lattice energy transfer is the T1 mechanism and does not describe loss of phase coherence.

body.prompt: How does T2* compare with T2?
options: T2* is shorter, since it adds field inhomogeneity
T2* is longer, since inhomogeneity slows the decay
T2 is shorter, since it adds field inhomogeneity
T2 and T2* are equal whenever a spin echo is used
body.explain: T2* includes everything that drives T2 plus dephasing from the magnet's static inhomogeneity, so the combined decay is faster and T2* is shorter. Adding a dephasing source can never lengthen the decay.

body.prompt: What does T2* decay include that pure T2 decay does not?
options: Dephasing from static main field inhomogeneity
Dephasing from neighbouring spin interactions
Energy loss from protons heating the lattice
Signal loss from the receive coil's bandwidth
body.explain: T2* adds the dephasing caused by the magnet's own field non-uniformity on top of true spin-spin dephasing. Neighbouring spin interactions are already what T2 measures.

body.prompt: The refocusing pulse in a spin-echo sequence has a flip angle of:
options: 180 degrees
90 degrees
45 degrees
270 degrees
body.explain: The spin echo uses a 180 degree pulse to flip the fanned-out spins so they rephase into an echo. The 90 degree pulse is the initial excitation, not the refocusing pulse.

body.prompt: For the echo to form exactly at TE, the 180 degree pulse must be applied at:
options: Half the echo time
The full echo time
Half the repetition time
Twice the echo time
body.explain: Rephasing takes exactly as long as the dephasing that preceded the flip, so the 180 sits at TE/2 and the spins come back into phase at TE. Placing it at TE would be after the echo was needed.

body.prompt: How does the 180 degree pulse produce an echo?
options: It flips the spins so fast ones trail, then catch up in phase
It halts all precession until every spin points the same way
It doubles the precession speed of the slower spins only
It tips the magnetization back along B0 to protect the signal
body.explain: The flip puts the spins that had gained phase behind the ones that had lagged; precessing at unchanged rates, the fast spins catch up and coherence returns at TE. The pulse never stops precession or changes any spin's rate.

body.prompt: Which signal loss does the spin-echo 180 degree pulse recover?
options: Dephasing caused by main field inhomogeneity
Dephasing caused by spin-spin interactions
Signal loss caused by incomplete T1 recovery
Signal loss caused by proton density variation
body.explain: The static field errors are the same before and after the flip, so their dephasing rewinds exactly; that is the T2* component. Random spin-spin dephasing is irreversible, so true T2 decay remains in the echo.

body.prompt: Why is a gradient-echo image more affected by field inhomogeneity than a spin-echo image?
options: It has no 180 pulse, so T2* dephasing is never refocused
It has no 90 pulse, so magnetization is never fully tipped
It uses a longer TE, so far more true T2 decay accumulates
It uses two 180 pulses, which cancel out the true T2 decay
body.explain: Gradient echo forms its echo with gradient reversal alone, which cannot undo dephasing from static field errors, so the signal decays with T2*. Spin echo's 180 pulse refocuses exactly those losses.
