body.title: Spatial encoding: slice, phase, and frequency gradients into k-space
body.html:
An MR signal on its own carries no address. Three gradients, switched on at three different moments of each TR, stamp position onto the signal. The slice-select gradient runs at the same time as the RF pulse. It makes the Larmor frequency vary along its axis, so only the plane of tissue whose local frequency matches the RF pulse gets excited. Slice thickness follows from two things: the RF bandwidth and the steepness of the gradient. A steeper gradient, or a narrower bandwidth, gives a thinner slice.

After excitation, the phase-encode gradient switches on briefly. Spins at different positions along its axis precess at different rates while it is on, and when it switches off they keep a position-dependent phase shift. The gradient is stepped to a different amplitude every TR, and each step writes one line of the raw data matrix. Finally the frequency-encode (readout) gradient runs during the echo itself, so that signal frequency encodes position along the third axis while the echo is digitised.

That raw data matrix is k-space. It is a map of spatial frequencies, not a picture. The central lines hold the low spatial frequencies: bulk signal, overall brightness, and contrast. The peripheral lines hold the high spatial frequencies: edges and fine detail. Every point in k-space contains signal from the entire slice.

Once every planned line is filled, a two-dimensional Fourier transform converts k-space into the image, turning spatial frequencies into pixel intensities. Excite, encode, sample, repeat per TR, transform: that is how every 2D image is built.
keypoints: The slice-select gradient is on during the RF pulse; only spins whose local Larmor frequency matches the RF are excited.
Slice thickness is set by the RF bandwidth and the steepness of the slice-select gradient.
The phase-encode gradient is a brief pulse after excitation, stepped to a new amplitude every TR; each step fills one line of k-space.
The frequency-encode (readout) gradient is on during the echo, so frequency encodes position while the echo is sampled.
k-space center holds contrast and bulk signal (low spatial frequencies); the periphery holds edges and fine detail; a 2D Fourier transform reconstructs the image.
body.worked_example: You run an axial brain series with 192 phase-encode steps. Each TR, the z gradient switches on with the RF pulse to excite the chosen slice, a phase-encode blip along right-left takes a new amplitude, and the readout gradient along anterior-posterior runs while the echo is sampled. After 192 TRs the 192 lines of k-space are full and the scanner Fourier transforms them into the image. The patient coughs halfway through, right when the central lines are being acquired. Because those lines carry the low spatial frequencies for the whole slice, the result is not a smudge at one spot but degraded contrast and ghosting across the entire image.
memory_hooks: Slice with the RF, phase in between, frequency while you listen.
Center of k-space = contrast; corners = crisp edges.
One TR, one phase step, one line.
exam_traps: The slice-select gradient is on during the RF pulse and the readout gradient is on during the echo; swapping the two is the classic error.
k-space center = contrast and signal, periphery = fine detail. Exams love to reverse them.
k-space is raw spatial-frequency data, not a scrambled photo: no single k-space point maps to a single pixel.

body.title: The image-formation pipeline: excite, encode, sample, reconstruct
body.html:
Every MR image, whatever the sequence name on the console, is built by the same loop. Excite the chosen slice with an RF pulse while the slice-select gradient is on. Encode the signal spatially: a phase-encode step, then frequency encoding during the readout. Sample the echo into one line of k-space. Repeat every TR with a new phase-encode amplitude until k-space is full, then reconstruct with the Fourier transform. Sequences differ mainly in how they form the echo that gets sampled.

A gradient echo sequence forms its echo by reversing the polarity of the readout gradient: the first lobe dephases the spins, the flipped lobe rephases them. There is no 180 degree pulse, so the signal decays with T2*, and the excitation typically uses a flip angle under 90 degrees, which leaves longitudinal magnetization in reserve and allows a very short TR.

A spin echo sequence forms its echo with a 180 degree refocusing pulse applied after the excitation. Inversion recovery adds a different 180: a preparatory inversion pulse placed before the excitation. After the inversion, the sequence waits a chosen time so that one tissue's longitudinal magnetization is crossing zero at the moment of excitation, and that tissue gives no signal. STIR uses this to null fat, FLAIR to null CSF.

Keep the two 180s apart: the inversion 180 prepares the magnetization before excitation, while the spin-echo 180 refocuses it afterward. And whatever the echo mechanism, they all end the same way: fill k-space, then reconstruct with a Fourier transform. A conventional scan fills one phase-encode line per TR; a fast or turbo scan fills several lines per TR (an echo train), which is how it saves time.
keypoints: Pipeline: excite the slice, phase then frequency encode, sample the echo into k-space, repeat per TR, Fourier transform to reconstruct.
Gradient echo forms its echo by reversing the readout gradient: no 180 degree pulse, T2* decay, flip angle usually under 90 degrees.
Spin echo forms its echo with a 180 degree refocusing pulse applied after the excitation.
Inversion recovery adds a preparatory 180 degree inversion before the excitation; the nulled tissue is excited at its zero crossing (STIR nulls fat, FLAIR nulls CSF).
Whatever the echo mechanism, the filled k-space is reconstructed with a Fourier transform; a conventional scan fills one phase-encode line per TR, a fast or turbo scan several (an echo train).
body.worked_example: You start a brain exam with a gradient-echo localizer: no refocusing pulse and a small flip angle let the TR drop to a few milliseconds, so the scout finishes in seconds, though the patient's dental work blooms because nothing refocuses the local field errors. Next comes a spin echo series, where a 180 degree pulse after each excitation forms the echo. Then the FLAIR: now a 180 degree inversion goes in before each excitation, with the wait time chosen so CSF is at its zero crossing and comes out black. Three different echo mechanisms, yet all three fill the same k-space matrix line by line and hand the filled matrix to the Fourier transform.
memory_hooks: GRE flips gradients, SE flips spins, IR flips first.
Excite, encode, sample, repeat, transform.
exam_traps: Gradient echo forms its echo by gradient reversal; there is no refocusing pulse in it to remove.
The inversion 180 comes before the excitation as preparation; the spin-echo 180 comes after it to refocus. Two different pulses, two different jobs.
One phase-encode line per TR is only the conventional case: a fast or turbo spin echo fills several lines per TR (an echo train), which is how it shortens the scan.

body.prompt: Which gradient is switched on at the same time as the RF excitation pulse?
options: The slice-select gradient
The phase-encode gradient
The frequency-encode gradient
The rewinder gradient
body.explain: The slice-select gradient runs with the RF pulse so that only one plane of tissue is on resonance. The phase and frequency gradients come later, after the slice is already excited.

body.prompt: An RF pulse applied while the slice-select gradient is on excites only one slice because:
options: only spins at that location precess at the RF frequency
only spins at that location align with the main field
the gradient shields the other slices from the RF energy
the receive coil is sensitive to that location alone
body.explain: With the gradient on, Larmor frequency varies along the patient, and the RF pulse tips only the spins whose frequency matches its own. Field alignment and coil sensitivity are the same for every slice, so neither can select one.

body.prompt: With the RF bandwidth unchanged, making the slice-select gradient steeper produces:
options: a thinner slice
a thicker slice
a noisier image
a brighter image
body.explain: A steeper gradient spreads Larmor frequencies over a shorter distance, so the fixed RF bandwidth maps onto a thinner band of tissue. A thicker slice would need a flatter gradient or a wider bandwidth.

body.prompt: The brief phase-encode gradient pulse leaves spins along its axis with:
options: a position-dependent phase shift
a position-dependent flip angle
a position-dependent T1 change
a position-dependent coil gain
body.explain: While the gradient is on, spins at different positions precess at different rates; when it switches off they keep a phase shift that tags their position. An encoding gradient changes neither flip angle nor T1.

body.prompt: In a standard 2D acquisition, each TR period fills how much of k-space?
options: One line
One pixel
One quadrant
The whole matrix
body.explain: Each TR acquires one echo under one phase-encode setting, which writes exactly one k-space line. Filling the whole matrix takes as many TRs as there are phase-encode steps.

body.prompt: A patient moves during the TRs that sample the central lines of k-space. The damage mainly appears in:
options: overall image contrast
fine edge detail only
the number of slices
the receiver bandwidth
body.explain: The central lines carry the low spatial frequencies that set overall contrast and brightness, so corrupting them degrades the whole image. Fine edges live in the periphery and would suffer if motion hit the outer lines instead.

body.prompt: A single data point in k-space represents:
options: one spatial frequency summed from the whole slice
one pixel at the same position in the final image
one slice location along the selection gradient
one coil element's share of the total signal
body.explain: Every k-space point stores the strength of one spatial frequency contributed by the entire slice, which is why k-space looks nothing like the picture. There is no one-to-one link between a k-space point and an image pixel.

body.prompt: Within one TR of a 2D sequence, the correct order of gradient events is:
options: slice-select, then phase-encode, then frequency-encode
phase-encode, then slice-select, then frequency-encode
frequency-encode, then phase-encode, then slice-select
phase-encode, then frequency-encode, then slice-select
body.explain: The slice-select gradient runs with the RF pulse, the phase-encode blip follows the excitation, and the frequency-encode gradient runs during the echo. This timing repeats every TR.

body.prompt: Which order matches the image-formation pipeline for one slice?
options: Excite, encode, sample the echo, reconstruct
Encode, excite, sample the echo, reconstruct
Reconstruct, excite, encode, sample the echo
Sample the echo, encode, excite, reconstruct
body.explain: The slice is excited first, spatial encoding is applied to the excited signal, the echo is sampled into k-space, and reconstruction happens last. There is no signal to encode or sample before the excitation.

body.prompt: The Fourier transform can reconstruct the image only after:
options: every planned k-space line has been sampled
the longitudinal magnetization fully recovers
the transverse magnetization fully decays
the gradients have returned to their baseline
body.explain: Reconstruction needs the complete set of spatial frequencies, so the transform waits until every planned line is in k-space. Relaxation happens every TR and is not what gates reconstruction.

body.prompt: During the readout period, the scanner's receiver digitises:
options: the echo, stored as one line of k-space
the RF excitation pulse as it is applied
the full image, one pixel at a time
the gradient waveform for that TR
body.explain: The receiver samples the echo while the readout gradient runs, and those samples become one k-space line. The scanner never digitises the image directly; the image exists only after the Fourier transform.

body.prompt: A gradient-echo sequence forms its echo by:
options: reversing the polarity of the readout gradient
applying a second RF pulse at half the TE
waiting for T1 recovery to rebuild the signal
stepping the phase-encode gradient amplitude
body.explain: Gradient echo dephases the spins with one readout lobe and rephases them with the flipped lobe, so no second RF pulse is needed. An RF pulse at half the TE describes spin echo, not gradient echo.

body.prompt: Compared with the 90 degree excitation of spin echo, gradient-echo sequences typically use:
options: a flip angle below 90 degrees
a flip angle above 90 degrees
a pair of 180 degree pulses
no excitation pulse at all
body.explain: Gradient echo usually excites with less than 90 degrees, which leaves longitudinal magnetization in reserve and allows a very short TR. Larger flip angles or paired 180s belong to other sequence types.

body.prompt: Which sequence family forms its echo with an RF refocusing pulse rather than a gradient reversal?
options: Spin echo
Gradient echo
Spoiled gradient echo
Balanced gradient echo
body.explain: Spin echo refocuses the signal with a 180 degree RF pulse. All the gradient-echo variants listed form their echoes by reversing the readout gradient instead.

body.prompt: In inversion recovery, the 180 degree pulse placed before the excitation serves to:
options: invert magnetization so a chosen tissue can be nulled
refocus dephasing so the echo forms exactly at TE
double the transverse signal before the readout
excite two slices at once to halve the scan time
body.explain: The inversion pulse flips magnetization negative before the excitation, and waiting the right time lets one tissue reach zero so it gives no signal. Refocusing at TE is the job of the spin-echo 180, a separate pulse with a different purpose.

body.prompt: STIR and FLAIR make their target tissue dark by timing the excitation:
options: when the tissue's longitudinal magnetization is zero
when the tissue's longitudinal recovery is complete
when the tissue's transverse magnetization peaks
when the tissue's resonant frequency is suppressed
body.explain: A tissue excited at the moment its inverted longitudinal magnetization crosses zero has nothing to tip into the transverse plane, so it appears black. If recovery were complete the tissue would be bright, not dark.

body.prompt: In a 3D volumetric acquisition, wrap-around along the slice-select (partition) direction is prevented by:
options: Oversampling in the slice-encode direction so tissue outside the slab does not fold into it
Lowering the receive bandwidth to widen the range of frequencies sampled at each partition
Shortening the echo time so that fewer partitions are needed to fill the excited slab
Raising the flip angle to saturate the signal from tissue beyond the edges of the slab
body.explain: A 3D acquisition phase-encodes the slice direction, so anatomy beyond the excited slab can alias onto the end partitions. Slice-direction oversampling extends encoding past the slab edges and discards the extra partitions, removing the wrap. Bandwidth, TE, and flip angle do not address slice-direction aliasing.

body.prompt: Compared with a single 2D slice, a 3D acquisition that phase-encodes the slice direction increases scan time mainly because:
options: Each partition adds a full set of phase-encoding steps, so the second phase axis multiplies the acquisition
The whole slab must be re-shimmed between every repetition to keep the partitions aligned
A longer echo time is forced on every partition to allow the slab to be excited fully
The receiver has to sample each frequency point several extra times to reach the same resolution
body.explain: 3D scan time is TR times the in-plane phase-encode steps times the number of slice-encode partitions (times NEX). The extra slice phase-encode loop multiplies acquisition time, which is why 3D usually pairs with short-TR gradient echo. Re-shimming, TE, and oversampled readout are not the reason.

body.prompt: Why can a 3D acquisition produce contiguous slices with no interslice gap, unlike a typical 2D acquisition?
options: The slab is partitioned by phase encoding rather than by separate selective excitations, so partitions do not need a gap to avoid cross-talk
The 3D readout gradient is strong enough to prevent any overlap between neighbouring slices
3D sequences are always run with a much longer TR, which lets each adjacent slice fully recover its longitudinal magnetization before the next excitation
The Fourier transform automatically inserts blank partitions between the reconstructed slices
body.explain: In 3D the slab is excited once and divided into partitions by a second phase-encoding gradient, so there is no imperfect slice profile overlapping a neighbour and no gap is needed. 2D uses separate selective excitations whose profiles overlap, which is why a gap or interleaving is used. Readout strength, TR, and the transform do not create the gap-free partitions.

body.prompt: A 3D acquisition tends to have higher SNR than an equivalent 2D acquisition mainly because:
options: Signal is collected from the entire slab on every excitation and averaged over all the slice-encode steps
The excited slab undergoes far less T2 decay than the individual 2D slices experience during their own separate readout windows
3D imaging uses a much larger voxel, which always raises the signal it receives
Gradient spoiling is unnecessary in 3D, so no transverse signal is ever discarded
body.explain: Because a 3D sequence excites and samples the whole slab for every slice-encode step, signal is effectively averaged over all partitions, giving an SNR gain that scales with the square root of the number of partitions. Larger voxels would raise SNR but are not the mechanism here, and the T2 and spoiling statements are incorrect.

body.prompt: In a contrast-enhanced 3D MR angiogram, a mask subtraction is performed by:
options: Subtracting a precontrast 3D data set from the postcontrast set so that only enhancing vessels remain
Removing every second partition from the postcontrast set to suppress the background tissue
Inverting the k-space of the postcontrast set before the Fourier transform to cancel the fat
Applying a saturation band over the aorta so that arterial inflow is nulled on the mask
body.explain: Subtraction MRA acquires a precontrast mask and a postcontrast set with identical geometry, then subtracts them so stationary background cancels and only the gadolinium-filled vessels remain. Dropping partitions, inverting k-space, and saturation bands do not produce a subtraction angiogram.

body.prompt: Reformatting a data set into an arbitrary oblique plane keeps full spatial resolution only when the source acquisition is:
options: 3D with isotropic voxels, because equal dimensions in all three axes reformat without blurring
2D with a large slice gap, because the gaps give the reformat room to interpolate cleanly
2D with thick slices, because thicker slices carry more signal into the reformatted plane
3D with a very high receive bandwidth, because bandwidth sets the through-plane resolution
body.explain: Isotropic 3D voxels have the same size along every axis, so a reformat in any plane preserves resolution. Thick 2D slices reformat poorly because the through-plane dimension is coarse and the oblique plane blurs. Slice gap and receive bandwidth do not give clean multiplanar reformats.

body.prompt: A balanced steady-state free precession (bSSFP) sequence is often run as a 3D acquisition because it:
options: Uses a very short TR with high signal, so the many partitions of a 3D slab can be collected quickly
Is immune to banding artifact, so field inhomogeneity across the slab never matters
Requires no gradient spoiling, which means it cannot be used for 2D imaging at all
Produces pure T1 weighting, which only becomes visible in a volumetric acquisition
body.explain: bSSFP has a very short TR and high signal efficiency, which suits the many slice-encode steps of a 3D slab and keeps total time reasonable. It is actually prone to banding from B0 inhomogeneity, can be run in 2D, and gives mixed T2/T1 contrast rather than pure T1.

body.prompt: In a 3D data set, k-space is filled along:
options: One frequency-encode axis and two phase-encode axes, one in-plane and one for the partitions
Three frequency-encode axes, one for each spatial dimension of the excited slab
One phase-encode axis only, with the other two directions taken from the readout
Two frequency-encode axes and a single phase-encode axis shared across all partitions
body.explain: A 3D acquisition frequency-encodes one axis and phase-encodes the other two, the in-plane phase direction and the slice (partition) direction, so k-space is a 3D matrix. The other options misstate how the three axes are encoded.

body.prompt: A drawback of STIR compared with spectral (chemical) fat saturation is that STIR:
options: Suppresses any tissue whose T1 is near that of fat, so enhancing tissue and some blood products are also nulled
Depends heavily on a uniform main magnetic field and fails badly wherever the field is inhomogeneous
Cannot be used at low field strength because the fat and water peaks are then too far apart
Requires a very long echo time, which unavoidably makes the whole sequence heavily T1 weighted
body.explain: STIR nulls signal based on T1, not on chemical frequency, so it is not tissue-specific: anything with a T1 near fat's is also suppressed, including gadolinium-enhancing tissue and some hemorrhage. Field uniformity dependence describes spectral sat, and the low-field and echo-time statements are wrong.

body.prompt: A practical advantage of the Dixon method over spectral fat saturation is that Dixon:
options: Tolerates field inhomogeneity better and yields water, fat, in-phase and opposed-phase images from one acquisition
Needs no reference to the fat and water resonant frequencies at all, so it can even be applied to nonproton imaging studies
Suppresses fat using a single inversion pulse and therefore takes much less time to run
Removes chemical-shift artifact by lowering the receive bandwidth used during the readout
body.explain: Dixon reconstructs water and fat from in-phase and opposed-phase data, so it is more robust to B0 inhomogeneity than frequency-selective saturation and produces four image sets at once. It still relies on the fat and water frequency difference, does not use an inversion pulse, and does not work by changing bandwidth.

body.prompt: The resonant frequency difference between fat and water protons is about 3.5 ppm, which at 1.5 T corresponds to roughly:
options: 220 Hz, and it roughly doubles to about 440 Hz at 3 T because the difference scales with field strength
70 Hz, and it stays the same at 3 T because a chemical shift in ppm is independent of the field
1000 Hz, and it falls to about 500 Hz at 3 T because higher fields narrow the separation
15 Hz, and it is far too small to be exploited by any frequency-selective saturation pulse
body.explain: At 1.5 T (about 64 MHz) a 3.5 ppm shift is roughly 220 Hz, and because the shift in hertz scales with field strength it roughly doubles to 440 Hz at 3 T. This larger separation is why spectral fat saturation is easier at higher field. The other values and their field dependence are incorrect.

body.prompt: On a 1.5 T gradient echo, fat and water signals are opposed in phase (India-ink boundary) at an echo time near:
options: 2.2 ms, with the two returning in phase near 4.4 ms as they precess back together
10 ms, with the two returning in phase near 20 ms after further dephasing
0.5 ms, with the two returning in phase near 1.0 ms during the first readout
50 ms, with the two never returning in phase because T2 star decay has removed the signal
body.explain: Fat and water differ by about 220 Hz at 1.5 T, so they are opposed in phase near 2.2 ms and back in phase near 4.4 ms. These in and opposed phase echo times halve at 3 T. The larger echo-time values given in the distractors do not match the fat-water beat period.

body.prompt: SPAIR and SPIR improve on a simple frequency-selective fat-saturation pulse mainly by:
options: Using a spectrally selective inversion that is more tolerant of B1 (transmit) nonuniformity than a plain saturation pulse
Nulling fat purely by its T1, so no knowledge of the fat frequency is needed at all
Acquiring two separate echoes so that the fat and water signals can be separated arithmetically after the scan is complete
Applying the fat pulse only to the center of k-space, which halves the added scan time
body.explain: SPAIR (and SPIR) use a spectrally selective inversion of fat, and the adiabatic version is relatively insensitive to B1 nonuniformity, giving more uniform suppression than a plain saturation pulse. They remain frequency-selective (unlike STIR), do not separate echoes arithmetically (that is Dixon), and are not limited to the center of k-space.

body.prompt: Fat stays relatively bright on fast (turbo) spin echo compared with conventional spin echo because:
options: The closely spaced refocusing pulses disrupt J-coupling in fat, which slows its T2 decay and keeps it bright
The long echo train lets fat recover far more of its longitudinal magnetization in between each of the successive echoes
Fast spin echo uses a much shorter effective TE, so little fat signal is ever lost
The multiple echoes average out the fat signal, which raises its apparent brightness
body.explain: The train of closely spaced 180 degree pulses in fast spin echo interferes with the J-coupling that normally speeds fat's T2 decay, so fat retains signal and appears brighter than on conventional spin echo. This is a common reason fat suppression is added to FSE. The recovery, effective-TE, and averaging explanations are incorrect.

body.prompt: First-order gradient moment nulling (flow compensation) corrects the phase of spins that are:
options: Moving at a constant velocity, leaving higher-order motion such as acceleration uncorrected
Completely stationary, so that only the fixed background tissue is rephased at the echo
Accelerating rapidly, which is the only motion that a first-order correction can address
Moving in random directions, so that fully turbulent flow is rephased at the readout
body.explain: Nulling the first gradient moment rephases spins moving at constant velocity, so flow-related dephasing from steady flow is corrected while acceleration and higher-order motion are not. Stationary spins are already rephased without it, and turbulent (random) flow is not corrected by a first-order scheme.

body.prompt: On a symmetric multi-echo spin echo sequence, even-echo rephasing describes how flowing spins:
options: Regain phase coherence on the even-numbered echoes, so those echoes show less flow-related signal loss
Lose all coherence by the second echo, so that the even echoes are always darker than the odd ones
Are fully saturated after the first echo, so that no vascular signal remains on any of the later echoes
Shift position between echoes, so the vessel appears in a slightly different place on each even echo
body.explain: With symmetric echo spacing, the phase that constant-velocity spins accumulate is undone on the even echoes, so flowing blood regains coherence and shows less signal loss there. It is a rephasing, not a saturation or a spatial shift, and it makes even echoes brighter for flow, not darker.

body.prompt: To reduce ghosting from blood flowing into the imaging volume, a spatial saturation band is best placed:
options: On the side the unwanted blood flows in from, so it is saturated before it enters the imaged slab
Directly over the region of interest, so the pulsing vessel inside it is nulled along with the ghosts
As far away from the vessel as possible, so that the saturation pulse cannot disturb the imaged anatomy
Only along the frequency-encode direction, since that is where the flow ghosts always propagate
body.explain: A pre-saturation band is placed on the side from which the unwanted blood enters (for example superior to the slab for descending venous flow), so the inflowing spins are already saturated and produce no ghost. Placing it over the region would null the anatomy, distance defeats the purpose, and flow ghosts propagate along phase, not frequency.

body.prompt: Increasing the number of signal averages (NEX) tends to reduce pulsatile flow ghosting because:
options: Averaging repeated acquisitions lowers the ghost intensity relative to the consistent true signal
A higher NEX shortens the total scan time, giving the pulsating vessel much less time to move
The extra averages move the ghosts into the frequency-encode direction, where they are hidden
Averaging raises the effective receive bandwidth, which spreads the ghost energy out of the image
body.explain: Ghosts arise from view-to-view inconsistency, so averaging several acquisitions reinforces the consistent stationary signal while the variable ghost contribution partly cancels, lowering ghost intensity. Higher NEX lengthens rather than shortens the scan, and it does not change the ghost direction or the bandwidth.

body.prompt: Respiratory compensation for body imaging can be achieved with all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Raising the flip angle so that the moving abdominal wall tissue no longer contributes any signal
A bellows that reorders phase encoding to the respiratory cycle (respiratory-ordered phase encoding)
A navigator echo that tracks diaphragm position and accepts data only within a set gating window
A breath-hold acquisition that is fast enough to freeze respiratory motion within a single hold
body.explain: Respiratory-ordered phase encoding (bellows), navigator echoes, and breath-holding all reduce respiratory motion artifact. Simply raising the flip angle does not suppress moving-tissue signal or compensate for breathing, so it is the exception.

body.prompt: Pseudogating, which can reduce pulsation ghosts without any physiologic monitor, occurs when the:
options: Repetition time happens to fall close to a multiple of the patient's cardiac cycle length
Echo time is set exactly equal to the duration of one full cardiac cycle of the patient
Receive bandwidth is deliberately matched to the frequency of the arterial pulsation
Slice thickness is chosen to be equal to the diameter of the pulsating vessel imaged
body.explain: If the TR coincides with (a multiple of) the cardiac period, each phase-encode view is sampled at the same point in the pulse cycle, so flow looks consistent and ghosting drops, effectively gating by accident. TE, bandwidth, and slice thickness do not create this effect.

body.prompt: Pulsatile flow ghosts appear as discrete repeating copies whose spacing along the phase-encode axis depends chiefly on the:
options: Ratio of the pulsation period to the repetition time, together with the number of phase-encode steps
Strength of the frequency-encode gradient that is used during the sampling of each echo
Overall receive bandwidth, which sets how far apart the copies fall in the readout direction
Absolute field strength of the magnet, which fixes the ghost spacing regardless of timing
body.explain: Because motion modulates the phase-encoded views, the ghost spacing is governed by how the pulsation period relates to the TR and the number of phase-encode steps. Readout gradient strength and bandwidth act in the frequency direction, and field strength does not set the ghost spacing.
